chapters.title: The Person in the Group Chat
The Wrong End of the Rink
A Field With Work to Do

call.title: The call dated tomorrow
call.text: The first call reached {{firstName}} before its speaker could make it. The speaker is still unknown.

holding.title: The temporary hold
holding.text: A precisely defined connection can be held temporarily. It cannot safely turn a person into a component.

deadline.title: The thirteenth interval
deadline.text: The accumulating messages will complete their circuit at first light on Sunday.

anubis.title: Anubis and the crossing
anubis.text: Anubis keeps a particular road and its passengers. His crossing is a choice, not universal authority over every part of the Duat.

records.title: A correction leaves evidence
records.text: The original false entry remains visible beside the record challenging it.

acknowledgement.title: Received without continuation
acknowledgement.text: Celia Bell’s message finished without claiming its receiver.

routes.title: Connections are directional
routes.text: A route, an address and a person are different subjects for a holding mark.

release.title: The release sequence
release.text: Two defined ends and an open refusal: loosen the agreement instead of cutting the body carrying it.

ren.title: Names and identity
ren.text: A name matters to a person’s identity. Miso’s chosen present name can make room beside a name used to bind him.

eva.title: Eva’s first call
eva.text: The first call had an end. Later imitations do not establish the same person.

original_call.title: The call she chose to finish
original_call.text: Eva left a message and chose to leave. Voss kept reopening its route.

wren.title: Wren
wren.text: She chose her own name. She carries intercepted voices but is not Eva Voss.

receiving_record.title: An independent receiving record
receiving_record.text: Wren can be recognised separately from the messages she carries.

reeds.title: A field with work to do
reeds.text: The Field of Reeds is encountered as a lived place, not a waiting room for somebody else’s grief.

wepwawet.title: Wepwawet: Opener of the Ways
wepwawet.text: Knowing which divine name and office to address can open an informed request. It does not confer ownership of a god.

true_mark.title: Nadia’s original receiving mark
true_mark.text: The false copy has a reversed final stroke. The original remains scratched underneath it.

returns.title: Three returns
returns.text: Mum knotted three return protections into my coat. A broken claim can spend one to bring me back. A cut or bruise cannot. The stitches are a working model, not three anatomical hearts.

birth_clue.title: The missing second signature
birth_clue.text: My birth-registration copy has a covered second signature. Leila thought it was a privacy measure. The ink continues under the covering.

repeated_refusal.title: The copied agreement
repeated_refusal.text: The same instruction treats an earlier answer as continuing agreement. I copied the fault without reopening its return.

counterledger.title: The counter-ledger
counterledger.text: The station records some refusals twice, then treats the repetition as renewed agreement. A separate list can demonstrate the alteration.

spirit_warning.title: The woman under the stair
spirit_warning.text: A waiting operator remembers a socket that Adrian hid. Listening let her recognise my return address too.

sun_trace.title: The route under the paint
sun_trace.text: Borrowed light made the workshop’s earlier route visible. The light revealed an alteration; it did not erase it.

self_terms.title: A road without a patron
self_terms.text: Dennis and I recorded a return by number, with no divine office signing for me. The work takes longer and needs another person watching the ordinary end.

heritage.title: The sealed birth record
heritage.text: Thoth is my divine father. Mum and he concealed his signature behind a witness seal to hide my return from the Exchange. Leila trusted the covered copy. His absence was a decision, not proof he could not help.

true_name.title: The unwritten part of my name
true_name.text: My ordinary name is {{fullName}}. Beneath it the register holds a private spoken cadence Mum used when I was small. I recognised it; I did not choose it in a menu. In this story, giving that complete cadence to an occupied line would expose its return. Egyptian ideas about ren inspired the rule; the register and its mechanics are fictional.

myth_note.title: Notes in Mum’s margin
myth_note.text: Thoth’s writing, healing and recording offices and Egyptian traditions about names inform the work. The Toronto Exchange, demigod family, return hearts and spell disciplines are our story’s inventions. The people on the line are not specimens of one uniform ancient Egyptian belief.

items.recorder: A copy of Nadia’s research recordings
items.connector: The spare connector from the first rescue
items.tested_torch: A checked torch and spare batteries

recap.text: I answered the first call.
I tried to silence the first call.
I delivered a private letter without reading it.
I left a letter waiting while I pursued the rescue.
I chose Julian over a useful component.
I put the false record on the record.
I kept my mother’s recording instead of obtaining a witness seal.
I stayed for Imani’s selection session.
I preserved Eva’s original goodbye.
I cleared the playback that could be used to imitate Eva.
Knowledge opened a road that force could not.
Trying to force the road left an injury.
I refused divine terms and took the flooded bypass.
I returned the voices and brought my mother home.
I saved those present and cut off unfinished messages.
I stayed to receive the voices under terms I chose.
Imani remembered the clue I denied having.
I asked Wren for help before treating her as a tool.
I preserved the counter-ledger; other families can challenge the repeated refusals.
I heard the waiting operator and accepted that she could hear me back.
Dennis held an ordinary return for me without a divine sponsor.
I accepted a limited obligation to the crossing office, with an end date.
My mastered Scribe Seal changed how the final load was carried.
The dead chose their own receiving roads.
I learned whose child I was. I kept the name {{fullName}}.
I broke my promise about the private cadence. Mum and Wren remembered.
One return heart remained.
The last return broke. My original playthrough remains available beside any chapter replay.
We used an ordinary witnessed return; no god inherited our decisions.
The counter-ledger changed the final load instead of becoming another item in my bag.

beats.text: I had checked the hallway before turning the lock. Mrs. Rinaldi's shopping trolley stood beside the lift, and somebody had left a wet glove on top of the recycling box. Nobody else was there. I remember this with the unfair clarity that arrives when I need a different explanation.
Now the phone is ringing in my hand, showing tomorrow's date.

It is Friday. I check the little date above the microwave, which has said January 1 since a power cut two winters ago. Useless. The laptop on the kitchen table says Friday. The chemistry worksheet underneath it says my name, {{fullName}}, and beside the first question I've written a number I already know is wrong.
Outside, someone knocks three times.

My aunt has a key. I tell myself she could have lost it. Leila loses pens, hair ties, the small scissors she buys to replace the small scissors she loses. She has never lost her keys. They hang from a bright orange strap marked EMERGENCY, which she chose because, in her words, nobody steals something that looks like a responsibility.
The sound comes again. Patient. I put the phone down on the counter without ending the call.
“Leila?”
“Open up, {{firstName}}.”
My own voice. Not a recording played back through a speaker. A person with my voice, out in the hallway, standing approximately where Mrs. Rinaldi parks her trolley.
I step away from the door. One of my socks catches a splinter in the laminate and makes a small, ordinary ripping sound.

Leila has spent eleven months making lists for me. Frightened? Call her. Can't sleep? Try that boring history podcast. Someone outside? Use the peephole, don't start an argument through the door. I have a plan for every emergency she can name, and no plan at all for this one.
Through the peephole, a person in my winter coat is holding a phone to their ear.

I know it is my coat because of the triangular patch near the pocket, where Mum fixed a tear with a scrap from an old curtain. A grey curtain with yellow birds. I had complained that it looked like something for a five-year-old, then refused to let her replace it.
The person raises their eyes to the peephole.
For a moment my brain does something embarrassing. It tries to make this a mirror. It adjusts the height, the angle, the shape of the light. Then the person smiles while my mouth stays open.
I cover the peephole with my palm.
On the kitchen counter, my phone says, “{{firstName}}?”
I don't remember deciding to pick it up.
“I'm here.”
The breath at the other end catches. Behind it, water runs over something hollow. A bell rings once, far away.
“Whatever happens,” my voice says, “do not open the door.”
I look at the door. The lock is turning slowly. I can see the little brass tab moving, fraction by fraction, although there is no key on my side.
“How do I stop it?”
“Blue notebook. Kitchen drawer.”
“What?”
“Mum's notebook. Get it. And {{firstName}}—”
The line goes dead.

For eleven months, adults have paused before saying my mother's name. My teachers do it. My dentist once did it with two fingers in my mouth, which made me briefly, furiously glad she hadn't gone into medicine. They say missing, and then wait to find out what version of that word I'm living with today.
The voice on the phone said Mum as if she could still come into the kitchen and tell me to stop picking the bird patch off my coat.
I open the drawer under the kettle.

Takeaway menus. A packet of birthday candles. Elastic bands Leila insists are useful, although their main function is to attach themselves to everything else. Under a bent photograph of me at a science fair lies a blue cloth notebook.
I've searched this drawer before. Twice. Once for a tin opener, once because I thought Mum might have left something my aunt hadn't found.
The notebook is warm.
I turn back its cover. Nadia {{surname}}, it says. If found, please return. Then her email address, the one I still sometimes write messages to and leave in drafts.
Beneath that, in a different pen: “{{firstName}}, if you're reading this, find Leila before you try anything clever.”

My knees go unreliable. I sit down on the edge of a chair and read the line twice. It is recognisably her handwriting, including the dot she always puts too far to the right of an i. I press my thumb against it, hard enough to crease the page.
The lock clicks.

I push the chair under the door handle. It fits badly. Leila has told the landlord six times that the kitchen chairs are too wobbly to use safely. Tonight I would like them to be considerably less affordable.
“{{firstName}},” the person outside says. “You left me out here.”
“You're wearing my coat.”
“So are you.”
I look down. The coat is over the chair at the table, exactly where I left it after school.
A little black paw appears outside the kitchen window and taps the glass.

I turn so quickly the notebook falls shut. On the fire escape sits a cat, fur puffed out against the cold. It has one pale whisker, a nick in an ear and the offended expression of an animal who has been waiting a long time.
It taps again.
I can hear the chair scraping across the floor behind me.
The window has been painted shut at the bottom. I hook my fingers under the frame and pull. Nothing. The cat mouths something through the glass. I stare at it.
It rolls its eyes, leans closer and says, distinctly, “Latch.”
I undo the latch.
The frame shoots upward. Cold air stings the wet inside of my nose. The cat climbs over the sill, shakes snow onto the chemistry worksheet, and pushes past me towards the notebook.
“Coat,” it says. “Phone. Shoes. Leave the laptop.”
I haven't mentioned the laptop.
“The expensive square,” the cat adds, impatiently. “Humans always go back for the expensive square.”
A screw falls from the door handle and bounces under the fridge.
I put on my coat. The real one, with the patch that catches on my thumb. I shove my feet into my boots, grab the notebook and phone, and climb through the window.
At the top of the fire escape, I look back.

My door opens three inches against the chair. In the gap I see my own hand, then an eye. The person inside my apartment looks towards the window. Its mouth moves. I can't hear the words over the traffic below.
The cat bites my sleeve and pulls.
I follow it down.

choices.label: Follow the cat down the fire escape

beats.text: The first landing is iced over. I discover this by sitting down on it extremely quickly.
Pain shoots up my left elbow. I manage to keep hold of the notebook. My phone slides three steps farther than I do and stops against a screw, which is the first useful screw I've encountered tonight.
The cat looks up from the next landing.
“Careful.”
I consider several responses. My aunt would not approve of any of them, though she uses the most efficient one when the hospital calls during dinner.
I get up slowly. The apartment window above me goes dark.

At street level the ladder ends eight feet above a collection of bins. I have lived in this building for four years without once thinking about the last eight feet of the fire escape. Clearly somebody on a planning committee thought fire would get bored before then.
“There's a release,” a voice says below me.
A girl in a red parka stands beside the bins, one glove raised. In her other hand she holds a hockey stick with a strip of blue tape around the blade.
“By your right foot. No, your other right.”

I find the catch. The ladder drops with a crash that sets off a car alarm halfway down the alley. The cat disappears under a skip. I climb down into a puddle deep enough to find the gap between my jeans and boots.
The girl watches me inspect the wet hem.
“You're {{firstName}}?”
I have just been warned not to open a door by someone wearing my face. This seems like a poor time to start confirming personal information.
“Who's asking?”
“Imani. Third floor. Your aunt sent me.” She takes out her phone. There is a message from Leila: “Can you check on {{firstName}}? Not answering. Don't go inside if anything seems off. Call me.”
Underneath it, Imani has written: Off how.
Leila hasn't answered.

I check my own phone. Four missed calls from my aunt. One incoming call labelled tomorrow, with no number attached. I try to show Imani, but the date changes back to today as soon as she leans closer.
“That's convenient,” I say.
“What is?”
“Nothing.”
She slips the phone into her pocket. “Right. Well, I'm on my way to my dad's shop. He can drive us to your aunt.”
“At two in the morning?”
“He's finishing a bus. I was awake. Why are you coming out of a window?”
The cat emerges from under the skip with a yoghurt lid attached to its back foot. It pauses to shake it off, fails, and turns its entire body to bite it.
“That,” I tell Imani, “is a longer answer.”
She follows my gaze. The cat freezes with the lid in its mouth.
“Is it yours?”
“No.”
“Then why does it look like you owe it money?”

I take a breath. A man with a takeaway bag passes the mouth of the alley, glances at the two of us and the ladder, and continues without slowing. The car alarm stops. Above me, one of the apartment windows opens. Somebody shouts that people have work in the morning.
I want to be that person. I would like my part in tonight's events to involve being briefly annoyed, closing a window and going back to sleep.
Imani shifts her stick to the other hand. “Your elbow's bleeding.”
I look down. A thin dark line has reached the edge of my cuff.
“It's fine.”
“I'm sure. Are you coming?”

I recognise her now. She and her dad moved into the third floor in the autumn. Leila took them food, then complained for a week that she'd given away her best container. I met Imani by the lifts and asked whether she went to my school. She said yes. I said cool. Neither of us could think of a second subject, so we watched the lift numbers together until she got out.
She knows my name because Leila uses it through the wall. I know hers because I once collected a delivery meant for her dad and kept forgetting to take it downstairs.
It occurs to me that, before tonight, this was approximately the amount of friendship I could manage without somebody asking how I was.
My phone rings.
Leila's face fills the screen, a photograph I took without warning while she was halfway through eating a peach. I answer so fast I almost drop it.
“I'm outside.”
“Outside where?”
“The building. There was someone—”
“Don't tell me your whole name. Don't tell anybody your whole name. Are you wearing the coat with the patch?”
I look at the bird.
“Yes.”
“Good. Keep it on. Imani there?”
Imani reaches for the phone. I put it on speaker instead.
“I'm here,” she says. “What's happening?”
Leila breathes out. In the background somebody calls for a porter.
“I need you both at the museum annex. The service door on the east side. Not the public museum. The little brick building across the lane. I'll send a pin.”
“Your shift?” I ask.
“I've asked somebody to cover.”
“Leila. There's someone in our flat.”
“I know.”
I stand very still. A drop of water falls from the end of the ladder onto my neck.
“How do you know?”
“We'll talk when you get here.”
“No. How—”
The call breaks into a rough crackle. I hear another voice through it, a girl's voice, very young. “Dad says don't tell them.”
Then the screen goes black.
Imani looks at me. The cat has stopped wrestling the yoghurt lid.
Behind the alley bins, the shadow cast by the streetlight lengthens until it reaches my boot. I move my foot. The shadow follows.
The cat drops the lid.
“Walk,” it says. “Don't run until you have to.”
For two seconds nobody moves.
Imani looks from me to the cat, then back again. She opens her mouth, closes it, and takes a firm grip on the hockey stick.
“Fine,” she says. “Museum. Talking later.”

choices.label: Ask Imani to come; share what I know

effects.detail: I asked for help instead of giving orders.

choices.label: Tell her to keep up; explain later

effects.detail: I ordered her to keep up in the alley.

beats.text: The pin Leila sends takes me to a brick building behind a locked vehicle gate. There is no sign saying museum annex, no golden mask on the door, nothing to explain why my aunt knows how to get in. A green wheelie bin lies on its side beside a pile of damp cardboard.
Imani presses the intercom.
A man answers, “Deliveries after eight.”
“Leila sent us.”
Nothing happens. I can hear a radio playing on the other side, followed by the scrape of a chair. Then the gate releases with a buzz.
“Nice security,” I say.
“The gate,” the man tells me through the intercom, “is on camera.”
I stop talking to the gate.

Inside the service entrance, the air smells of radiator dust and cardboard. A security officer sits behind a desk with a half-completed crossword. He has written the same answer in two different places and is frowning at one of them.
“She's downstairs. Don't touch anything. Cat stays out.”
The cat walks between his shoes.
He looks down at it. “You again.”
“Evening, Dennis.”
Dennis removes his glasses, rubs the bridge of his nose and puts them back on. “I've told them about this. They still won't put it in the incident form.”
Imani and I follow the cat before Dennis remembers we were supposed to be doing something ordinary.

The basement stairs end at a fire door propped open with a crate of bottled water. Leila stands beyond it in her navy scrubs, coat unbuttoned, her hair escaping its clip. She has one of the hospital's small cardboard cups in her hand. When she sees me she puts it down without finding a surface. It falls and spills coffee across the floor.

She hugs me first. I don't decide whether to let her. Her arms close around my shoulders and my face presses into the clean hospital smell of her sleeve, and for a second I stop holding myself upright.
Then she takes my elbow.
“Sit.”
“I'm fine.”
“Sit while being fine.”

She cleans the cut with something from her bag. It hurts more than I expect. Imani leans her stick against the table and watches the door. The cat starts washing its chest as if it has done all the work available.
“You knew,” I say.
Leila peels the backing off a dressing.
“About that thing in the flat. You said you knew.”
“I knew it might try.”
The cat stops washing. Imani looks at me, then discreetly studies a shelf of archive boxes.
“How long?”
Leila presses the dressing down too firmly. I flinch, and she loosens her grip.
“Since your mum went missing.”

There is a notice on the wall asking staff to separate paper and plastic waste. I read it three times while she tells me that my mother studied things she couldn't put in published papers. That the little brick building stores equipment which isn't part of the museum's public collection. That some of the work happened here, after hours, with permission from people who knew enough to sign the right forms and not enough to be useful now.
“You let the police look for her.”
“Yes.”
“You let me go with them.”
“{{firstName}}.”
“I showed them her favourite coffee place.”
Leila puts the unused half of the dressing packet into her pocket. “I remember.”
I pull my arm away. “Were you ever going to tell me?”
She looks towards Imani. I hate her for that small glance, for measuring how much can be said in front of somebody else.
Imani picks up her stick. “There's a vending machine upstairs. I'm going to call my dad.”
Nobody asks her to leave. She goes anyway, letting the fire door close behind her with a gentle click.
Leila waits until it has shut. “I didn't know whether Nadia was alive.”
“But you knew where she'd gone.”
“I knew the name of a place. I couldn't reach it.”
“You could have told me that.”
“Yes,” she says.
The answer is so plain that for a moment I have nothing to put against it. I had prepared for excuses. I've spent eleven months listening to people explain how little information they can give me.
I put the notebook on the table. Her face changes when she sees it.
“Where did you find that?”
“In the drawer. Where you keep the menus.”
“It wasn't there.”
“I know.”

She sits down opposite me. Her hand hovers above the cover without touching it. I see a faint white scar across the inside of her wrist, one I asked about last summer. She said she'd burned herself with steam.
The cat jumps onto the table.
“He needs the diagram,” it says.
Leila's expression hardens. “You need to tell me how you got out.”
“I walked.”
“You don't walk.”
“I've been practising.”
Something taps against a cupboard door on the far wall. The cat lowers itself until its belly touches the table. Leila gets up at once.
“Stay there.”
Of course I don't.

Inside the cupboard is an old brass bell, the kind with a little button on top. It sits on a saucer of salt. Beside it lie a battery recorder, a length of cut telephone cable and a photograph of a girl in a yellow raincoat. Somebody has folded the photograph so tightly that a white line runs across the girl's face.
The bell's button pushes down.
Leila catches it before it can release.
A voice comes from the recorder, although its screen is off. I recognise the small voice from the interrupted call.
“Dad says we're not ready.”
The cat backs into my leg.
Leila holds the bell so tightly her hand shakes. “{{firstName}}. Open the notebook. First blue tab.”
I do. Under the tab is a drawing of a circle crossed by three short lines. One of the lines is broken. Beneath it, Mum has written: Temporary hold. Seven minutes maximum. Never use on living tissue.
I show Leila.
“I know what it looks like. Draw it.”
“With what?”
She nods at a box on the shelf. Inside are sticks of white chalk wrapped in tissue. My fingers close around one and come away dusty.
I copy the circle on the cupboard's inside wall. The chalk squeaks. Nothing happens. Leila makes a small sound through her teeth.
“Close the end. It's open at the bottom.”
I repair the gap.
The bell stops moving. Leila takes her hand away. A red mark has appeared across her palm.
On the table, my phone lights up.
A message from an unknown number reads: “Your mother is tired. We should discuss this before somebody makes a mistake.”
The name beneath it is Adrian Voss.

I know the name Voss. It is on a plaque beside a lift in the museum, and on a Christmas card Mum used to stand behind the kettle because she didn't like the picture on the front. A silver deer, I remember. A deer with legs too long for the envelope.
Leila reads the message and turns my phone face down.
“Don't answer.”
“That's what everyone keeps saying about phones tonight.”
She takes a breath, stops, and goes to fetch another chair. There are several things she wants me to do with the chair, judging from the care with which she positions it. Sit. Stay still. Be younger.

Instead I open Mum's notebook. Behind the diagram I used is a map with three names I recognise and one I don't. The annex. A disconnected exchange room. A service building near the waterfront. The fourth name is written in a careful hand: Duat.
The cat puts a paw on the page.
“Other side,” it says. “Complicated place. Don't assume every door goes to the same part.”
“You're going to explain why you talk at some point.”
“I'm Miso. I talk because I have things to say.”
“You could say them better.”
Miso looks at Leila. “He's definitely hers.”
I'm not ready for anyone to make that observation, even a cat. I push his paw off the notebook.
Imani returns with a paper cup of hot chocolate and a packet of plain crisps. She sets the crisps beside me.
“My dad's coming here at five. He's finishing the bus first. He thinks your aunt's car broke down.” She looks at Leila. “I'd like to keep the rest of the lie small.”
Leila nods once. “You should go home with him.”
“Probably.” Imani sits on the table instead of the chair. “What was the ringing?”
Nobody answers quickly enough.
“Okay,” she says. “Still doing that.”

I turn the notebook so she can see the map. Leila's lips press together, but she lets me. I tell Imani about the double and the voice on the phone, including the part where it sounded like me. Saying it aloud in a lit room makes it sound less believable. Imani asks whether I checked the call log, then remembers she already watched me try.
Miso walks over the map.
“Nadia left a return address. We need to know whether it still receives.”
“Where?” I ask.
“The old exchange room. We take the streetcar.”
Leila begins to object. Miso looks towards the bell cupboard, where the chalk mark is already turning grey at its edges.
“If you leave that unattended,” he says, “we'll be finding out how many people in this city answer unknown numbers.”

She looks at me. I can see how badly she wants a reason to say no that I will accept. At last she takes my phone and enters a number, then presses a brass feather into my palm. It is small enough to fit between two fingers, with a hole drilled through the stem.
“Your mother's. Keep it. Call me from the exchange room, not on the way. If the screen starts showing dates it shouldn't, put it away.”
“Is Mum alive?”
“I don't know,” she says. “I am going to tell you what I know, even when it's that.”
I put the feather in the chalk box. It doesn't feel like enough to trust her with.
Outside, the cold has sharpened. Imani buys two fares from a machine while I try to work out what a cat pays. Miso climbs into the fold of my coat, apparently resolving the question.
The streetcar arrives almost empty. I check the destination display before boarding. It shows the right street, then a string of characters I can't read, then the right street again.
“We sure?” I whisper.
“Quite sure we shouldn't stand here,” Miso says from inside my collar.
Imani goes first. The driver holds up one hand.
“What did you leave behind?”
She looks at the fare reader. “We're paying.”
“Different question.”
The driver's face is hidden under the brim of his cap. His hands rest on a wheel that streetcars do not normally have. Behind him, rainwater moves upward across the windscreen.
Imani steps back until her elbow touches mine.
“The fare is an honest account,” the driver says. “Something unfinished. Something you can still name without taking it from anybody else.”
“Can we get off?” I ask.
“Yes.” He nods towards the open doors. “While they're open.”
That helps. I hadn't realised how badly I needed to hear a choice was actually mine.

choices.label: Tell the driver what I really left behind

effects.detail: I offered an honest fare at the crossing.
I asked what the crossing would claim.

choices.label: Claim I left nothing; risk losing the transfer

effects.detail: I gave a false account at the crossing.

choices.label: Push past the barrier; risk an injury

effects.detail: I tried to force my way past the divine barrier.

choices.label: Name the limits of the fare before he can define them

effects.detail: I made him define the limits before giving an account.

choices.label: Refuse the fare and use the longer exit

effects.detail: I refused the fare and accepted a longer road.

beats.text: The streetcar crosses a bridge I cannot see. Its wheels make the regular clatter of tracks, but beneath the windows there is only water and the occasional pale shape moving against the current.
The driver has put his cap on the dashboard. Above his seat, a brass card reads ANUBIS. I look back out at the water before deciding to ask another question.
Imani is still holding her fare.
“Do I need one of those transfers?” she asks.
“You'll need to tell me where you're going,” Anubis says.
“The exchange room.”
“Not an address I would recommend.”
Miso climbs from my coat onto the empty seat opposite. “The child has a return line.”
“Then the child should learn to use the return line.”
“Everyone's a teacher when they're driving.”
Anubis looks at him in the mirror. Miso lowers his ears and stops talking.

The boy holding the bread gets up at the next stop. Through the open door I see a narrow platform, a lamp and a woman standing with both hands over her mouth. The boy runs to her without looking back. By the time the doors shut, the platform has gone.
I lean forward.
“Can you take us to my mum?”
“No.”
The answer comes without hesitation. I wish he'd taken a little longer to find it.
“Don't you know where she is?”

“I know what your guide told me. I also know there are roads which turn anyone who travels them into part of the toll. I'm responsible for the passengers who use this road. That doesn't give me authority over every broken thing connected to it.”
He indicates the seats behind me. The woman with the suitcase looks away before I can meet her eyes.
I sit back. I hadn't realised I was asking him to leave other people waiting.
Miso paws at the transfer in my hand. The stamp looks like a feather enclosed by a rectangle. Under it, in ordinary English, someone has written RECEIVED WITHOUT SUBSTITUTE.
“Keep that,” he says.
“What substitute?”
“Ask the man who sent you a message.”

I look at the place where a stamped transfer might have been. Miso follows my gaze. “We can still find the door,” he says. “Don't assume the route will remember us as invited.” I put the blank fare ticket in my pocket and leave the thought there with it.
Imani has been watching the river. “Does everybody end up here?”
Anubis takes a long moment before answering her.
“People have imagined many roads. People have needed many roads. This is one of mine.”
At the next stop he opens the doors and points to a concrete staircase.
“Up. Keep to the rail. Don't answer anyone who asks you to hold their place.”

I want to ask what happens if I do. Miso is already out of the streetcar, his claws clicking on the concrete. Imani follows. I thank the driver, feel foolish thanking a god as if he's held a door for me, then feel more foolish for thinking the two things should cancel each other out.
“{{firstName}},” he says.
I turn.
“An address brings you to a door. It doesn't decide whether you open it.”
Before I can ask if that is advice about the call, the doors close.
At the top of the stairs I find a locked metal door. Beside it is a disconnected payphone. The receiver hangs crookedly from a cord wrapped in silver tape.
Miso jumps onto the little shelf under it. “Notebook.”
I find the return address. It isn't a building number. It is a sequence of six marks, three of which I recognise from the temporary hold.
“Say them?” I ask.
“Dial them.”

The keypad has no numbers. When I look closely I can see scratches where numbers should be, shapes that rearrange when I stop concentrating. I turn the notebook to match their orientation and press the sequence.
The call connects on the fifth mark.
“No,” Miso says quickly. “Finish it.”
A woman's voice says, “{{firstName}}?”
My finger stops above the last key.
“It's Mum. Listen. I don't have long.”

I know the voice. It has the little rough place at the bottom that arrived after she had a winter cough three years ago. I know how she says listen before telling me where she put something I should already have found.
Imani touches my wrist.
“Six marks,” she says. “There are six.”
The receiver has gone warm.
“Mum?”
Miso's claws press into the back of my hand. He isn't hurting me. He is close to it.
“Last mark.”
I press it.
The voice cuts off halfway through my name. A mechanism turns inside the door, and a young man on the other side pulls it open.
He is wearing a cardigan with one elbow held together by safety pins. His hair is flattened on one side as if he has been asleep against a book.
“You nearly sent your return line through an open channel,” he says. Then he notices Miso. “Oh, good. It's your fault.”
“Julian,” Miso says.
“Don't Julian me. I've been here since Wednesday.”
He lets me in. Beyond the door lies a room full of empty telephone booths. Their glass panels reflect a sky full of stars, although there are no windows.
One booth at the back is lit. In it, a telephone rings beneath a handwritten sign.
DO NOT PICK UP TO SEE WHO IT IS.
Underneath, someone has added: YES, THIS MEANS YOU, JULIAN.
Julian puts the kettle on, checks the water level, and takes it off again.
“Never mind. It might be river water.”

I follow his gaze to a stain on the ceiling. It has the shape of the building above me, though the building changes while I watch. A chimney disappears. A fire escape grows down through one edge. My own kitchen window opens briefly in the middle.
“Is that how you saw the flat?” I ask Miso.
He jumps onto a desk and settles his tail over his paws. “One way.”
Julian makes a sound that suggests there are several worse ways.

He is nineteen, he tells me, studying part-time and working for the small independent archive attached to the annex. He says independent with a care that suggests he has already had to explain it to a tax office. Most of the collection is ordinary: old operator manuals, repair logs, donated equipment. The part that isn't ordinary has been making his working week increasingly difficult.
“My supervisor used to deal with that bit.”
“Nadia?”
He nods.
“You knew my mum.”
“I still know her.”
For that sentence alone, I could forgive him a lot. He seems to realise he has offered something larger than he meant to, because he begins moving papers into neat piles.
The lit booth rings again.
Imani points to it. “What happens if somebody picks up?”
“Usually someone asks for somebody who isn't there. If you tell them they're wrong, they try the next place. If you offer to help, the system decides you're available.”
“Available for what?”
Julian looks at Miso.
The cat answers. “To carry the message.”
He says it as if that should explain everything. I wait until he notices I haven't understood.
“The original line let a caller send a message without making the receiver answer. Whoever built this version removed that safeguard.”
Julian takes a recorder from a drawer. It is the same model as the one in the annex. A strip of tape on its back says NADIA: BACKUP.
My mother speaks when he presses play.

“Test forty-three. The holding mark remains temporary. Seven minutes if the line is stable. Less if it isn't. We need a second reader at the receiving end. Adrian says we can automate the acknowledgement. I disagree.”
A pause. A paper being turned. In the background I hear myself, younger, complaining about homework. Julian stops the recorder when he sees my face.
“Sorry.”
“Play it.”
“There's quite a lot.”
“Play it.”

Mum's voice returns. She describes a circuit she has been testing, then corrects herself, then starts the explanation again without recording over the first attempt. I have spent months trying to preserve every memory I have of her. Here she is getting annoyed at a loose battery cover.
I need to sit down. I do it before anybody asks.
The recording ends with her saying, “{{firstName}}, don't put that near the—” and a loud clatter.

I remember the day. I dropped a screwdriver into a ceramic mug she'd been using to hold broken components. I thought she was angry because it was her favourite mug. Now, listening to the quick movement afterwards, I wonder what else was inside it.
Julian slides the recorder across the desk.
“Keep it. It's a copy.”
“Why haven't you given this to Leila?”
His mouth tightens.
“Because I couldn't get back through the door until someone dialled the full return address. I did tell you about Wednesday.”
Miso examines a paw.
I take the chalk from its box. On the desk I draw the holding mark, exactly as I drew it in the cupboard. Julian sets an old desk fan beside it and plugs the fan into a socket. Nothing happens.
“Magic doesn't work because chalk is expensive,” he says. “That shape holds a relationship. You need to tell it what relationship.”
I point to the notebook. “It doesn't say that.”
“It does. In the little note you skipped.”
It does. I skipped the note because it looked like a caption.

He puts my hand on the fan's plug, then makes me describe the connection between the socket and the motor. I say electricity. He asks what electricity is doing. I say making the fan spin. He asks what I want to stop.
“The fan spinning.”
“Then you want the mechanism, not the connection.”
Imani, who has been crouching beside the fan, turns its power switch on. It begins to rattle.
“Or that,” Julian says.

I let go of the plug. I want to laugh, but the room has started to feel unfair. My mother did something here that kept her away for eleven months. There should be a more difficult explanation than a switch I didn't notice.
Julian tears a sheet of paper in half and writes YOUR END on one piece, MY END on the other. He gives one to me.
“Try it on something that needs two people.”
I put the paper on the desk. Imani holds the second half. When I close the final line of the chalk mark, the two pieces rise an inch from the wood and stay there.
My fingers ache. I concentrate on the torn edges, on where they would fit together. The paper begins to shake.
“Breathe,” Imani says.
I breathe. The pieces settle.
Julian starts a timer. I hold the mark for forty-one seconds before my hand cramps and the papers fall.
It feels like failure until he writes forty-one in the margin beside my mother's first test.
Her time was twelve seconds.
At the back of the room, the ringing phone stops. A printer I hadn't noticed begins feeding out paper. Julian reaches it before the sheet can fall.
Three lines are printed across the top.
RECEIVING POINT CONFIRMED.
NADIA {{surname|upper}}: CONNECTION ACTIVE.
COLLECTION SCHEDULE: SUNDAY, FIRST LIGHT.
It is Friday morning. I have two days.
The collection schedule gives me a deadline and no address. I turn the paper over as if the missing information might be on the back.
Julian takes it away before I wear a hole through it.
“We have to trace an earlier call. Same receiving point, older sender. There'll be an acknowledgement.”
“An address.”
“If the operator kept records.”
“Did she?”
He raises one eyebrow at the notebook in my hand.

Miso leads me to a booth with a cracked pane. Behind the glass, a telephone sits beside a sewing basket. An empty chair faces a window full of afternoon sunshine. It is bright enough to make my eyes hurt after the long night.
“This was Celia Bell's,” Julian says. “A volunteer operator. She died before the connection broke. Her channel's been replaying because the last message never reached its destination.”
“Where's Celia?”
“Gone on. This is what she left.”
He doesn't offer a simpler explanation. I am beginning to appreciate that about him.

The door opens into a flat full of warm air and the smell of something baking. A radio plays softly in the kitchen. There are birthday cards on the mantelpiece, several months of them displayed together. On the table beside the telephone lies an envelope addressed to a man called Martin.
A woman in a green cardigan sits by the window. When I come in, she looks up and smiles.
“Are you from the pharmacy?”
“No,” I say.
“I rang yesterday. They said they'd send somebody.”
Imani stays in the doorway. Miso sniffs the woman's shoes, then moves to the telephone.
The woman doesn't react to him. She repeats her question.
“Are you from the pharmacy?”
I understand then, a little. The room is starting over. The radio plays the same two notes. The kitchen clock clicks back from twelve to eleven.
On the envelope, the ink of Martin's name runs down the paper.
Julian points towards a cabinet behind the woman's chair. “Routing book. We need the entries for last March.”

I could walk around her. She isn't watching me; her gaze is fixed on the door, waiting for a person who must be taking a long time. But her hand rests on the cabinet's drawer, and when Julian tries to open it she grips the handle.
“Private papers.”
“We need to help someone.”
“Private papers,” she says again.
I look at the letter. The envelope hasn't been sealed. A faint rectangle marks the place where a stamp should be.
“Who is Martin?” I ask.
The radio stops.
“My son.”
“Can we deliver your letter?”
For the first time her eyes follow me. They are a cloudy blue, with the red rims of someone who hasn't slept well.
“He doesn't answer the phone.”
“Do you have his address?”
She gestures to the envelope. The street name has almost disappeared. I write it down before it can go entirely.
Julian shifts his weight. “{{firstName}}. We can't start taking on every—”
“I said can we. I haven't said I will.”
Mrs. Bell looks towards the kitchen. A timer sounds once and dies.
“I told him not to come,” she says. “He was driving in that weather. I said it could wait until Tuesday.”
I sit on the edge of the sofa. The cushion has a dent where someone must have sat for years.
“Did he come?”
“No.”
She looks relieved, and then unhappy, and then relieved again. The room doesn't seem able to decide which part to keep.
Imani takes out her phone. There is no signal, but she types the address into a note.
“We can find out whether he still lives there,” she says. “That's a thing we can actually promise.”
Mrs. Bell releases the drawer.

Inside, the routing book is an ordinary ledger with ruled columns. Most of the entries are numbers. In the margin beside Nadia {{surname}}, a small cross has been drawn through the return line. Under it, my mother's writing says: Received at lower station. Witness present: A. Voss. Ask why he didn't sign.
I photograph the page. On my screen, the photograph shows only a blank ledger.
“Pen,” Julian says, passing me one. “Paper holds. Cameras copy the wrong layer.”
I write the entry in my notebook, including the little cross and the exact position of the unsigned box.
The woman reaches for the letter. Her fingers go through it.
“Oh,” she says.
The afternoon light thins.
Miso stands beside the door, tail rigid. “We should leave.”
The room has begun to tilt. Cups slide across the mantelpiece. Imani catches my sleeve as the sofa shifts away from the wall. I take the envelope with my other hand and pull back towards the booth.
Mrs. Bell has stopped looking at me. She is watching the window.
“Tell him it wasn't because I didn't want him,” she says.
I cannot tell whether she's asking me or remembering a conversation she already had.
Back in the exchange room, the glass pane cracks from top to bottom. The flat goes dark. My watch says six minutes and forty-eight seconds have passed.
I still have the letter.
Julian closes the booth door carefully.
“You're going to need to decide,” he says, “which promises fit in two days.”
I put the envelope inside the notebook, where the address won't rub away.

choices.label: Keep the promise: take the letter to Martin

effects.detail: I delivered Celia Bell’s letter without reading it.

choices.label: Keep the letter safe; return to Leila first

effects.detail: Celia Bell’s letter is still waiting to be delivered.

beats.text: The letter has an address on a street Julian says isn't far from the exchange room's ordinary exit. It is still early enough that the shops have their shutters down. I stand under an awning while a delivery driver drags crates into a bakery and wonder whether showing up at a stranger's house before seven counts as a worse idea when the letter comes from his dead mother.
Imani checks the note in her phone.
“We can leave it. We promised to find out whether he lives there. Not make him open it.”
Julian is carrying the evidence box against his chest. He has been looking at the time every few minutes.
“Your aunt thinks we're on our way back.”
“So tell her where we are,” Imani says.
I do. Leila replies with an address confirmation and a request to stay together. No lecture. It is almost more difficult to argue with.

The house has a small front garden full of snow-covered pots. Two bins stand by the side gate. A light is on in the kitchen. Through the glass beside the door I can see a coat rack with far more coats than the space was designed to hold.
I ring once.
A man in slippers opens the door. He looks at the three of us, then at the box, then at Miso. His hand stays on the latch.
“Yes?”
“Martin Bell?”
“Who's asking?”
Fair question. I give my first name and explain that the letter was found among papers belonging to his mother. It is a careful explanation. I don't enjoy how much it resembles Leila's earlier ones.
He looks at the envelope.
“My mother died in November.”
“We know.”
He takes it, examines the handwriting and leans one shoulder against the door frame. For a moment he seems too tired to keep being suspicious.
“Where was this?”
“In an archive,” Julian says. “She worked as a volunteer operator. We're cataloguing a group of personal papers.”
Not entirely true. Not entirely false. Martin looks at the box again and accepts enough of it to stop asking at the door.
He doesn't invite me in. I am glad. It means I don't have to explain which part of my reason for being there is a trespass into his life.
He turns the envelope over. The back is unsealed.
“Did you read it?”
“No,” I say.

I could have. In the exchange room, during the long wait for the door. In Dennis's car. On the pavement. The notebook has been full of things I needed to know, and it would have been easy to put the letter in the same category.
Martin nods once. He opens it while I stand on the step. His eyes move quickly over the first lines, then stop.
Behind him, someone in the kitchen asks whether he needs help. He says no without looking away from the page.
I feel I should leave. Nobody has told me to leave. I have become very aware of the wet soles of my boots and the small stone under one heel.
Then Martin folds the letter.
“She kept telling me not to drive in the snow,” he says.
I don't answer. I know something he hasn't asked me to know, and saying it would make me the owner of a conversation that belongs to him.
He looks at the envelope again.
“I was angry. I thought she didn't want help. She always made it sound like a nuisance, having somebody come over.”
Imani shifts beside me. Julian studies a crack in the step.
Martin rubs his thumb along the fold.
“Thank you for bringing it.”
“You're welcome.”
He goes inside. The door closes gently. I hear a chair move in the kitchen, then another voice, too low to understand.
On the pavement, I take out my notebook to mark the promise complete. My pen hovers above the page.
Julian says, “Don't write what he said.”
“I wasn't.”
I had been about to. Not from malice. It was a clue, a response, something that might help explain the system. I close the notebook and put it away.
Miso walks beside the garden wall. His paws make four precise prints in the new snow. I watch them until the next patch of cleared pavement makes them disappear.

At the corner, Imani buys three small buns from the bakery. Julian says he doesn't want one, then eats half before remembering he said that. I stand under the awning, eating warm bread while the delivery driver restacks his empty crates.
“Was it worth the time?” Julian asks.
I think of Mum in a room I haven't reached yet. The deadline. The narrow places a day can acquire when I'm afraid of using it badly.
“I don't know how to count it.”
He accepts that. I am grateful he doesn't tell me the answer should be obvious.
On my phone, the routing entry for Celia Bell changes. A small line of text appears beneath it: received without continuation.
I show Julian. He stops eating.
“That,” he says, “is what the acknowledgement is supposed to look like.”
I write down those words. Not Martin's letter. Not his grief. Just the part the line has given me permission to see.
When I reach the annex, Leila is standing outside the door. She looks at the time, at the three of us, and then at the bag from the bakery.
“Any left?”
Imani hands her the last bun. My aunt eats half of it before asking for the report.

Leila collects me from the service door of a building I could have walked past a hundred times. She has borrowed Dennis's car, an elderly hatchback with a child seat in the back and a packet of wet wipes in every available pocket.
“Dennis has grandchildren,” she explains when Imani asks.
“I wasn't asking about the wipes.”
“No,” Leila says. “Sorry.”

Julian sits in the front. He has to hold a cardboard box in his lap because the passenger footwell is full of additional wet wipes. Miso stays inside the box with the flap partly open. Nobody has suggested he needs to hide; he seems to prefer being luggage to being questioned.

I am home before nine. The flat looks ordinary from the doorway. The chair I wedged under the handle is back at the kitchen table. The screw from the handle sits beside my laptop. Someone has laid the chemistry worksheet neatly on top of it, although I left it on a streetcar which crossed a river under the city.

Leila checks the rooms before letting me in. She uses a little mirror from her bag, turning it towards each corner. I want to ask how she knows what to look for. I want to go straight to bed and wake up yesterday.
There is a note on the table.
“You have my face in the mirror. I'd like it back.”
It is written in pencil. The letters have the careful shape of someone copying them from a sign.
Miso sniffs it, sneezes and climbs onto the windowsill.
“Don't destroy it,” Julian says.
“I wasn't going to.”
“You look like you want to.”
I put the note under an empty glass.

Imani's dad arrives while Leila is making toast. He is broad-shouldered, tired, and wearing a work jacket with a rip at the cuff. He looks first at Imani, then at Leila, then at me. His eyes stop on the dressing at my elbow.
“Car trouble?” he says.
Leila turns off the toaster.
“A situation at the building. I needed Imani to help {{firstName}} get out.”
“What situation?”
“The door wouldn't open safely.”

I can see her searching for a statement that is accurate enough to survive. I used to think grown-ups had some private source of better explanations. Watching my aunt choose each word, I begin to suspect that a lot of adulthood is deciding how much trouble the next sentence will cause.
Imani's dad doesn't like the answer. He doesn't have time to stay and dislike it properly. He tells Imani to get her bag.
She says, “I need to come back later.”
“For what?”
“Helping.”
“Helping somebody else miss school?”
“Dad.”
“Selection is tomorrow. You told me that was important.”
“It is.”
“Then eat. Sleep. And answer your phone.”
She takes the toast Leila offers and wraps it in a paper towel. At the door she looks back at me, waiting for something.
I realise I haven't thanked her.
“Thanks.”
She gives a short nod. It isn't quite the response I wanted, but I'm not sure what response I earned.
After she leaves, Julian telephones his college and says he has a family emergency. He doesn't stumble over the lie. When he catches me looking, he covers the receiver.
“My manager won't write 'trapped in another realm' on a reference.”
Leila calls my school. I hear her say medical issue, family situation, expected back Monday. The office person asks a question that makes her close her eyes.
“No. We don't have an update about Nadia.”
I leave the kitchen before she can finish.

My room smells of the orange peel I left on the desk yesterday. The bed is unmade. A clean school shirt hangs from the wardrobe handle because Leila refuses to put away clothes I am perfectly capable of putting away myself. Everything in the room is arranged around a person who thought they knew how Friday would go.
I sit on the bed and take off my boots. My socks have dried stiff at the ankles.
In my phone's drafts is the last message I wrote to Mum. I open it.
“Leila bought the wrong cereal again. I know you'd say it's the same cereal in a different box. It isn't. I can tell.”
There is no ending to the message. I always got stuck there. How do I say goodbye to an email address when I've spent months insisting I'm only saying see you later?
I delete nothing. I close the draft.
On the other side of the wall, Julian and Leila are talking quietly. I can make out my name, Voss's name, the word lower. A chair scrapes. I press my face into the pillow, angry at how tired I am.
When I wake, someone has put a glass of water by the bed. The flat is silent except for Miso snoring on my clean shirt.
It is two in the afternoon.
My phone contains a message from Imani: Don't do the important bit without telling me.
Underneath is a second message.
Seriously.
I lie there with the phone balanced on my chest. Then I reply: Haven't found the important bit yet.
The typing indicator appears immediately.
“You could start by asking.”

By the time Imani returns, Leila has covered the kitchen table with paper. Hospital forms, archive printouts, pages copied from the notebook. She has weighed the corners down with tins because the radiator makes a draft she doesn't trust.
Julian has drawn a map on the back of a grocery receipt. It is not a reassuring map. Arrows lead into boxes labelled POSSIBLY STORAGE and DO NOT ASSUME STAIRS.
“I thought you worked there,” I say.
“I work in the part where we catalogue telephones.”
He turns the receipt over. On the other side, between onions and detergent, is a name written several times. Ruth Park.
“My sister,” he says before I ask. “I'm supposed to remember her wedding.”
“You forgot?”
“I traded a memory for access to an address book. I meant to give away a Wednesday afternoon. The person taking it said that was fine.”
“What happened?”
“I didn't specify which Wednesday. Or who I was with. Weddings aren't always on Saturdays.”
He folds the receipt so the name disappears.
Leila reaches for a pencil. “We're not bargaining with anyone.”
“Depends what they're asking,” Imani says.
My aunt gives her the look she uses when a patient has found a treatment on the internet. Imani returns it without seeming especially concerned.

I open the ledger copy from Mrs. Bell's flat. Nadia's entry has two boxes: sender present and receiving witness. Voss's name appears in the second. There should be a signature underneath. Instead somebody has crossed the return line out.
Miso walks over the papers and sits beside it.
“That isn't a cancellation,” he says.
“What is it?”
“A diversion.”
Julian leans close. The pencil work is difficult to separate from the ruled line beneath it. He follows the marks with the blunt end of his pen.
“He sent her connection somewhere else.”
The kitchen feels too warm. I pull at the collar of my coat, which I haven't taken off since waking.
“Where?”
“The lower station. But the route's been renamed. We need its first designation.”
“Then we ask Voss.”
Leila shakes her head. “Adrian will tell you enough to make you do what he wants.”
“He's the only person who's offered to talk.”
The words land where I intend them to. I'm not proud of the small relief that follows.

My aunt puts the pencil down. “He paid for the first equipment. He designed most of the line controls. Your mother needed a way to hold two incompatible signals apart, and he had spent half his working life solving exactly that kind of problem. At first it was useful.”
“And then his daughter died.”
Leila's eyes narrow. “How do you know that?”
I show her the photograph from the cupboard, which Julian brought in his box. The girl in the yellow coat stands beside a woman whose face has been cut out of the picture.
“Eva,” Leila says. “His wife left him after the funeral. Don't invent a story about that. I don't know why she left.”
Imani picks up one of the printouts. It is a donor report, neatly formatted, with Voss's full name and the date Nadia stopped signing the weekly test sheets.
“Eleven months,” she says. “Why is it starting now?”
Nobody has an answer ready.
Then Julian takes the bell diagram and turns it ninety degrees. The twelve scratches around its edge align with twelve smaller marks in Mum's circuit.
“They're holding intervals. Not months exactly. Load cycles.”
He draws a thirteenth mark. It crosses all the others.
“When the last interval closes, every waiting message tries to complete at the same time.”
I think of the boy with the bread. The woman waiting on the platform. The person wearing my face.
“How many?”
Julian doesn't write a number. He puts his pen down.
I take my phone out before anybody can tell me not to. Voss's message is still there. This time it displays a number. I press call.
He answers on the second ring.
“{{firstName}}. Is Leila with you?”
“Yes.”
“Good. I'd prefer she heard this too.”
That is an intelligent thing to say. I dislike him a little more for saying it.
“Where's my mother?”
“Alive. I spoke to her this morning.”
Leila holds out a hand. I don't give her the phone.
“Put her on.”
“I can't from here. I can show you the direct line. But I need you to come to the gallery on Harbord. Four o'clock. Public place. Bring whoever you need to feel comfortable.”
“Why not come here?”
“Because Miso will prevent you listening.”
The cat doesn't look away from the phone.
Voss continues. “You'll hear some very alarming things about me. Several are true. Ask yourself why nobody else has brought your mother home.”
The call ends.
Imani watches me set the phone down. “He's good at that.”
“I noticed.”
“Did you?”
I want to tell her I'm not stupid. Instead I look at the timetable on her screen, which she has been checking between sentences. Saturday morning. A rink address. A time in bold.
“You don't have to come.”
“I know.”
“You keep saying that.”
“Because you keep saying it like I don't.”
She takes the receipt map and puts it inside her phone case. It is a small practical act, and the argument I was preparing has nowhere sensible to go.

At the bottom of one routing sheet, a note specifies that diverted calls carry the next reserved receiving date, not the time of the speaker. I copy it because it may explain tomorrow on my phone. It does not yet explain whose voice I heard.

c09a.title: The Person in the Group Chat

beats.text: My friend Ella messages while Julian is sorting the gallery numbers. She sends a photograph of the chemistry board, followed by a second photograph because the first is blurred.

I haven't replied to her last four messages. I meant to. At first I didn't know what to say. Then replying required explaining why I hadn't replied, and the explanation became another message I couldn't finish.
Now she writes: “Your aunt said medical. You okay?”
I type yes, delete it, and type: At home. Family thing. Thanks for the notes.
Three dots appear.
“You don't have to do a whole update. Just send a full stop sometimes so I know you're not dead.”

I stare at the screen. The word dead looks different when someone uses it carelessly. It also looks like a word a friend might use because she has no idea how to ask the careful question without sounding like everybody else.
I send a full stop.
Her reply comes immediately: Incredible. Communication.
I laugh before remembering I am supposed to be frightened. It is a small sound, but Julian looks up.
“Something useful?”
“Yes,” I say. “Not about this.”

c09a~1.title: The Person in the Group Chat

beats.text: I take the phone into the sitting room and call her. She answers with, “Oh. A voice. Didn't know yours still worked.”
“Sometimes.”

She tells me about school. Someone has moved my locker contents because the hinge broke again. My chemistry teacher has decided to give everyone an extra week on the project, which Ella calls a personal apology from the universe. A boy I don't particularly like has been saying things about my attendance. She tells me she dealt with it, then refuses to specify how.
For several minutes I am allowed to be irritated by the correct small things. I sit on the floor beside the sofa and pick at a loose thread while she complains about the cafeteria's attempt at soup.
Then she says, “Someone rang my mum last night. Asked for you.”
My hand stops.
“Who?”
“Didn't say. Mum thought it was school. At three in the morning, so obviously not school, but you know how people sound official and she starts finding a pen.”
“What did they ask?”
“Your full name. Whether she knew where you were.”
I get up.
“Ella. Did she tell them?”

c09a~2.title: The Person in the Group Chat

beats.text: There is a pause. “I don't think so. Why?”
I go to the kitchen door and beckon Julian. He sees my face and puts his papers down.
“I need you to ask her. Don't call the number back.”
“{{firstName}}?”
“I know it sounds strange. Please don't call it back.”
Ella goes quiet in a way that is worse than a question. I hear her walk into another room and speak to her mother. The answer comes through indistinctly. Then Ella returns.
“She said she didn't know. She told them to call your aunt.”
I close my eyes.
“Okay. That's good.”
“Why?”
Julian holds out a scrap of paper. On it he has written: If they have a voice, they try its connections.
I think of my unanswered messages. The group chat. A person asking after I because she wants me to show up in class, accidentally becoming a line the Exchange can use.
“I can't explain all of it yet,” I say. “Something happened with Mum's work. Somebody is trying to get information through people who know us.”
That is true enough to sound worse than the version involving a talking cat.

c09a~3.title: The Person in the Group Chat

beats.text: Ella says, “Do I tell somebody?”
“Your mum. My aunt. Yes.”

Leila has come in behind Julian. I pass her the phone. She gives Ella a number for Dennis, then says the calls are part of an ongoing safety problem and should not be answered. She doesn't tell Ella she imagined anything. I hear the care in that choice.
Afterwards, Ella asks for me back.
“You could've told me there was a problem.”
“I didn't know how.”
“I didn't ask for a perfect explanation.”
I sit down again. The loose thread has wrapped around one finger so tightly it has left a red line.
“I know.”
“Do you?”
I unwind the thread.
“I think I'm starting to.”

She tells me she will keep the notes. If I need to miss another week, say so. If I don't want people asking questions, say that too. She doesn't promise to make everyone behave. She does promise to send a full stop at lunch.
I agree to send one back.

c09a~4.title: The Person in the Group Chat

beats.text: When the call ends, Julian adds Ella's household to the map. He writes only the information needed to block the diverted request, then puts the rest of the page facedown.
I recognise the distinction from Mrs. Bell's letter.
“I don't want everyone I know pulled into this.”
“Then we give the line fewer ways to mistake concern for permission.”

He shows me how to mark a receiving refusal on an ordinary piece of paper, tied to a number rather than a person. Leila calls Ella's mother and talks her through it as an unusual precaution. I can hear how odd the instructions sound. I can also hear the other woman deciding to do them anyway.
For the next twenty minutes I copy the mark onto cards for the households Leila knows have received calls. It is repetitive work. My hand gets tired. Nothing dramatic happens.
When one of the lines on Julian's map goes dark, I keep working.
I check each refusal mark for a leak before Leila calls the next household. The last card holds without my hand beside it.
I listen only long enough to tell whether the caller is still present, then close my end. Ella’s mother has not agreed to carry another voice.
I borrow the desk lamp to find the overwritten digit on the final refusal card. I wait for the after-image to fade before checking it with Julian.
I give the empty test request a decoy and close it before Leila uses the real number.

effects.detail: I helped Ella’s household refuse a diverted call.

beats.text: The gallery sells landscape paintings and very expensive lamps. Through the window I can see a blue lake rendered in thick paint, with a small red canoe positioned to make the blue seem bigger. I spend a moment wondering whether the painter has ever been in a canoe before remembering that I have come to confront a man about my missing mother.
Voss is waiting at a table near the back. He gets up when I enter.
He looks ordinary. This annoys me. His coat is hung neatly on the chair. His shirt has a pale stain near one cuff. There is a loose thread on his scarf which he keeps trying to tuck out of sight.
“{{firstName}}.” He looks at Imani. “And?”
“Imani.”
“Tea?”
“No.”
She says it before I can decide whether refusing tea makes me look more suspicious than accepting it.

Leila stands behind my chair. Miso has refused to enter the gallery, which Voss notices without asking about. I can see the cat through the window, sitting beside a planter and watching a pigeon with excessive concentration.
Voss takes a small device from his bag. It looks like a dictation recorder with a brass socket fitted into its side.
“Your mother's line. One-way for now. She won't hear you.”
I look at Leila. She nods, reluctantly.
He presses a switch.
Mum is humming. Very badly. A tune I remember because she never got past the same four notes. Something clicks. She says, “No, that won't hold,” then swears softly enough that I have to lean closer.
I cover the lower half of my face with one hand.
Leila reaches for the device. Voss lets her inspect it. She listens, checks a tiny movement in the brass socket and sets it back down.
“It's live,” she says.
Mum hums the four notes again.
“Can you tell where?” I ask.
“The lower station,” Voss says. “She made herself part of the holding circuit. I have a way to relieve her.”
Leila looks at him. “With what?”
“A willing replacement.”
“No.”
“I haven't asked {{firstName}}.”
“You don't need to.”
The woman at the front of the gallery glances over. Voss lowers his voice.
“I meant myself.”
I look at him properly for the first time.
He lets the silence sit. He is very good at leaving a space I want to fill for him.
“Why haven't you?” I ask.
“The station won't accept the person who diverted its first return line. There needs to be a witness to alter that restriction. A relative of the person holding it would be strongest.”
“Strongest,” Imani repeats.
“A connected witness.”
“You could've said that.”
Voss smiles at her without showing his teeth. “Yes.”
Leila leans forward. “You told Nadia the acknowledgement controls were manual. She trusted you.”
“They were manual.”
“You fitted a bypass.”
“To make the system stable.”
“To make it ignore refusals.”
He looks down at the loose thread on his scarf. For a moment the mild expression slips.
“People say things when they're afraid.”
The room stays quiet. On the recorder Mum says a number, corrects it and starts over. I know how she sounds when she has been working too long. She is there now.
“Eva,” I say.
Voss looks up.
“The little girl. That's who you're trying to bring back.”
His hand closes around the edge of the table.
“That's private.”
“So was Mum.”
Leila puts a hand on my shoulder. I move out from under it without thinking. Voss sees that too.

He takes a photograph from his wallet. Eva stands in the raincoat, front tooth missing, holding a small snow globe. The woman cut out of the other picture is present in this one, her arm around Eva's shoulders. She looks tired and happy and not like an explanation for anything.
“She hated snow,” he says. “Until it stopped. Then she wanted it back. Every year.”
I wait.
“I heard her through one of Nadia's early tests. Just a word. My name.”
“Did she ask you to do this?”
His eyes go flat.
“Would you have ignored your mother?”
It is the wrong question, and it still works. I look towards the recorder.
Voss pushes a card across the table. On it is an address and a time: lower entrance, six p.m. He has written the time by hand.
“You can investigate without me. I expect you will. But I have access she needs. Don't let somebody else's account of me cost you another chance.”
Outside, Miso is standing with all four paws planted against the pavement.
Voss follows my gaze. “Ask him about the collar. Ask whose name keeps it closed.”
Mum's voice stops. I reach for the recorder before I can stop myself.
Voss turns it off.
“I'll leave you to discuss it.”
He gets up, pays for four cups of tea nobody ordered, and leaves through a side door.
For a while I sit with the photograph he forgot on the table. Then Leila turns it over.
On the back, under Eva's name, is a short list of numbers. One has been crossed out and replaced. I copy all of them.
Imani notices. She says nothing until we're outside.
“You were listening,” she says.
“You sound surprised.”
“I was worried.”
It is a different answer. I keep it to myself instead of making a joke.

choices.label: Show Imani the copied numbers now

effects.detail: I shared Voss’s extra information before using it.

choices.label: Say he gave me nothing else; keep the clue

effects.detail: I denied having Voss’s extra clue.

beats.text: Julian finds the first number from Voss's photograph in a disconnected catalogue. It refers to a room the archive no longer owns, in a building demolished before I was born.
“Helpful,” Imani says.
“The room might still be there.”
She waits for the rest of that sentence. Julian takes off his cardigan and puts it back on as if that will make the explanation easier.
“Addresses don't disappear at the same speed as buildings.”
Miso leads me through the back of a laundrette. The owner looks up from folding towels, sees Julian and says, “If you're going downstairs, bring up my trolley.”
Julian promises to try. Outside the basement door he stops me.
“I'm not promising anything else in there. I've already lost enough.”

The stairs end in a market built from shelves. High above me, light falls through a roof of catalogue cards. People move along narrow aisles with bags held close to their chests. A man is selling keys without teeth. A woman has arranged glasses of water around a notebook. Every time she turns a page, someone whispers through the glasses.
I keep my hands in my pockets.

At the centre stands a desk broad enough to eat dinner on. Behind it a man with a long, narrow face is writing in three books at once. His left hand turns a page. His right continues writing. A third pen moves without anyone holding it.
Miso sits at a respectful distance.
The man doesn't look up. “The trolley's behind the north shelves, Julian.”
“I didn't ask.”
“You were going to. And your earlier request remains under review.”
Julian's face shuts down.
I put the copied number on the desk. The third pen stops.
“A diverted address,” the man says. “Whose permission do you bring to examine it?”
“My mother's.”
“Did she give it?”
I look at the notebook. Mum wrote my name in it. She told me to find Leila. She didn't tell me to come here.
“No.”
“Then tell me whose permission you bring.”
“Mine.”
“That I can record.”

The man draws a line under my number. When he turns his head, his shadow on the shelf has a long curved beak. I remember a school project, a picture of an ibis, my mother's patient explanation that the gods had more than one form and people should stop treating the heads like a matching quiz.
“Thoth?” I ask.
beats.speaker: {{firstName}}

beats.text: “Among other ways of asking for my attention.”
beats.speaker: The witness

beats.text: “I need the address.”
“You need access to the record of its alteration. Those are different requests.”
Imani rests her hands on the edge of the desk. “What do we have to pay?”
“An account which corrects the record.”
“That's vague.”
“It becomes less vague if you stop offering me objects I have no use for.”
I hadn't offered him anything. He looks towards the notebook under my arm, and I tuck it closer before I can help myself.
Thoth sets one of the three books in front of me. In the first column are names. In the second, brief statements. In the third, the spaces where signatures should be.
He taps a line.
NADIA {{surname|upper}}. EXTENDED VOLUNTARY SERVICE. AUTHORITY TO DELEGATE RECEIPT.
The signature underneath resembles my mother's. It is too tidy. Mum always let the last stroke trail into whatever space was left. This version stops exactly where the ruled box ends.
“That isn't what happened,” I say.
“Then submit evidence.”

I take out the letter from Mrs. Bell's flat. The ledger copy. Mum's recording. On their own they explain pieces. Together they show who was present, who changed the route and when my mother stopped signing.
Thoth listens to the recording without expression. When Mum swears at the battery cover, the third pen makes a small mark in its book.
“You can file these,” he says. “They will be retained until the dispute is settled.”
I hold the recorder tighter. It has her voice on it. I only just got it.
Julian puts his own recorder beside mine.
“Copy,” he says. “Remember?”

I could trust the process. I could try to steal the book and run, though every aisle looks the same and the person behind the desk has been turning pages without using his hands. I could refuse the terms and try Voss's lower entrance, knowing less about what he plans.
Thoth waits. He doesn't make the decision easier by being kind.
Behind me, a trolley rolls slowly out of a side aisle and nudges Julian's ankle.
“Thank you,” Julian says stiffly.
“Ask me for something I can return,” Thoth tells him.
Julian looks down at the handle. For a moment I think he's going to argue. Instead he takes the trolley and pushes it towards the stairs.
I look back at the disputed signature. Mum's name shouldn't be sitting in a book beside a sentence she never agreed to.
I keep one hand on the recorder while I decide.

choices.label: Submit the evidence; receive a witness seal

effects.detail: I submitted evidence to challenge the false entry.

choices.label: Keep Mum’s recorder; leave without a seal

effects.detail: I kept the evidence and accepted an uncertified route.

choices.label: Try to steal the book; risk the witness’s trust

effects.detail: I tried to steal the record I wanted corrected.

beats.text: Imani taps the place where I copied the numbers. “You said there was nothing else. Next time tell me before the locked door.”
The correction doesn't make the lie disappear. Thoth rules a narrow line through it, leaving every letter legible, and attaches a reference number to the evidence.
“People will still be able to see it?” I ask.
“They need to see what was changed.”
He writes a second address beneath the first. The marks look simple until I try to copy them. One seems to belong behind another, although they're both on the same page.
Julian turns my notebook sideways.
“Write the order separately.”
I make six small numbered boxes. Thoth watches me fill them.
“Take the witness receipt,” he says. “You may challenge a delegated authority once. It will not hold the door open for you. It will make the door ask the question it was told to skip.”
I fold the receipt along its printed line. It is longer than my pocket, so I fold it twice more. Nobody says anything about the untidy result.

The address on the public card takes longer to copy than I expect. Without a witness seal, every redirected mark has to be checked against the notebook. Julian helps without claiming I have proof I chose not to submit. I write the missing receipt on a separate line so nobody can mistake the address for one.

On the way out, Imani buys a bottle of water from the laundrette. Ordinary water, from an ordinary fridge, with an ordinary price she objects to before paying it. Julian helps carry the trolley up the stairs. The owner says, “Finally,” and gives him a packet of biscuits.

We sit on the laundrette's front step and pass the biscuits between us. It is nearly six. The sky has the flat purple colour it gets before snow, and the bus shelter across the road is crowded with people trying not to touch.
Julian takes one biscuit, then breaks it and puts half back.
“Ruth doesn't know,” he says.
I turn towards him. He keeps looking at the road.
“About the wedding. I let her think I was drunk. The photographer sent me the pictures. I know where everyone stood. I can describe the cake.”
“Doesn't that help?”
“It makes me better at lying about it.”
The laundrette door opens behind me. Warm air and the smell of soap spill over the steps. A woman carries a bag past me without looking down.
Imani asks, “What did you need the address book for?”
Julian rubs the biscuit crumbs off his hand.
“Nadia. After she disappeared. I thought I could find her before anybody noticed how much I didn't know.”
I hadn't expected that. I thought he would say a rare book, or a promotion, or a door he shouldn't have tried. Something that would make the price easier to judge.
“I didn't know you,” he adds. “It wasn't for you.”
“Okay.”
“She took me seriously. At work. That's all.”
He says that's all in a tone that makes Imani stop asking questions.

Miso is crouched under the step, watching a delivery cyclist fix a dropped chain. His collar has appeared around his neck. I haven't seen it before. Thin black leather, too tight at the throat, with a brass plate tucked under the fur.
I remember what Voss said.
“Whose name keeps it closed?”
The cat goes still.
Julian looks up sharply. “Don't.”
“Voss told me to ask.”
“Voss tells everybody something true when he wants them to stop noticing the rest.”
Miso stands and walks towards the alley. I get up after him.
“I wasn't—”
He moves faster. I follow him around the corner, leaving Imani and Julian on the step.
At the end of the alley, he turns.
“Yes,” he says. “I worked for him.”
“Doing what?”
“Opening doors. Carrying messages. Finding people he said were lost.”
“My mother?”
The question hangs there long enough to answer itself.
I sit back on a low wall. My elbow throbs where the dressing pulls against the cut.
“You took her there.”
“She asked me to.”
“Did she know you worked for him?”
“No.”
A rubbish bag shifts in the wind. Miso watches it instead of me.
