When the sequence is finished, Leila checks it against the original.
“You left out the limit.”
Voss says nothing.
“The return window,” she says. “How long?”
“Seven minutes.”
“Under current load.”
He looks towards Wren, who is sitting on the inside step with Miso beside her.
“Four,” he says.
Julian crosses out seven.

I read the new figure. Four minutes to hold the broken connections, ask the questions the bypass removed, release my mother and bring everybody through. After two days of searching, the answer fits inside a number I can count on one hand.
Voss gets up.
“I can hold the master line. From inside.”
Leila looks at me. This time she doesn't decide in advance which answer I am allowed to hear.
I look at Voss's hands. No cable burns. No grey skin. He has found ways to stay outside the machinery he built.
“If you come,” I say, “you don't get a private channel.”
He nods, reluctantly.
“And if Wren says no, she means no.”
He looks as if he might argue about the name again. Then he picks his phone up from the chair and puts it in his pocket.
“All right.”
I do not mistake the words for a guarantee. Julian writes them down anyway.
Wren asks which reflection is supposed to carry the next decoy. “A blank one,” I say. She waits while Julian verifies that it is actually blank.

Imani lays the torch between us. “The reflection trick got us out. I still want a warning before you make a second version of someone I’m trying to follow.” She leaves her hand on the ordinary torch until I answer.
Julian looks at the spare connector, then at his bandaged hand. “Tell me before you choose a piece of equipment over the person holding it.”
Julian checks the reader, then meets my eyes. “You pulled me out. I can hold this end.”
Nobody likes rehearsing an emergency. Leila says this while making everyone do it a third time.

Julian has arranged the equipment on two tables. The bell case is at one end, the second reader at the other. Between them lie paper cards representing Nadia, the waiting messages, Wren, the witness, and the operator. He has drawn a little cat on the card for Miso. Miso has been trying to sit on it ever since.
“You're not a load-bearing component,” Julian tells him.
“Good. Finally.”

Voss stands near the door. Dennis watches him from a chair, holding a mug with both hands. There is no realistic reason a retired security officer with a mug should intimidate Voss. It appears to be working anyway.

The first rehearsal fails because I close the holding mark before Imani positions the reader. The second fails because Julian changes a setting with the wrong hand and knocks the lever out of alignment. The third fails because Wren says she isn't ready and everyone else takes too long to stop.
“We stop when she says it,” I say.
Voss turns towards me.
“If we stop at the wrong time—”
“Then we need to know what stopping means before we're in there.”
I hear Leila's teaching voice in my own. It is irritating and useful.

Julian marks three stages on the table with tape. Before the first, I can withdraw. Between the first and second, the system holds temporarily. After the second, the messages have begun to separate; stopping then means choosing another way to contain them.
“What other way?” Imani asks.
“Break the bell,” Leila says. “Sever the crossing. It will get us out, but unfinished messages will lose the only route we know how to reach.”
Wren looks at her card. Her name is written in Julian's cramped hand beside the words independent receiving record.
“And me?”
“The record should keep you separate,” Julian says. “I can't promise what the shock will do.”
I appreciate the honest sentence and hate the uncertainty inside it.

Voss takes a pen and points to the operator's card. “There is one further option. A live receiver could hold the load while the rest of you disconnect. With the bypass removed, it would no longer be forced.”
Everyone looks at him.
“Yes,” he says. “I am aware.”
Mum held it for eleven months. I think about how Voss has arranged the possibility so it sounds newly reasonable now that he has said willing.
Julian puts a second card underneath the operator.
“One person. No ordinary way out. We'd have to build a new receiving point from outside.”
“We don't choose that by accident,” Imani says.
“No,” Leila agrees.

We rehearse again. This time Wren says stop halfway through, and all of us stop. Miso takes his paw off the cat card. Julian lowers the lever. Imani sets the reader down. I open the outer line of the mark without breaking the inner one.
Nothing falls. Nothing is trapped. Wren breathes out and looks almost embarrassed by her relief.
We go again. At the end, Julian checks the timer.
“Three minutes and twenty-eight seconds.”
Imani looks at the table. “Thirty-two spare.”
“Only if nobody argues,” Dennis says.
Voss does not look at him.

Leila packs the equipment. She labels everything in large letters, including the bag containing chalk, which nobody was likely to confuse with anything else. I do not tease her. I have started to understand how much fear can fit inside being organised.

Miso noses the edge of my notebook. A page I haven't read falls open. On it, Mum has sketched several jackal figures in different poses. Beneath one she has written Wepwawet, Opener of the Ways. Beside the name is a note: Ask for a road, not ownership of the road. Courtesy isn't payment. Precision matters.
I read the name aloud carefully. Miso looks towards the door.
“He may be there,” he says. “When the lower route narrows.”
“Does knowing the name help?”
“Knowing which name to use helps. Don't assume any name gives you command.”
I mark the page with a strip of blue tape. Imani does the same to the release diagram, then hands the roll back without saying anything about whether she trusts me to remember it.

Near midnight, Dennis brings the car around. Leila checks every latch on the bell case. Voss carries the equipment bag under Imani's supervision. Julian signs the archive's paper register before leaving, including an estimated return time.
I look at the blank line after his signature.
“You think they'll care?”
“I will,” he says.
I write my name under his. My ordinary name, in my ordinary handwriting, with a pen that is running out of ink. Then I close the register and follow the others out.
In the dry run I share the small seal across two prepared surfaces. When Julian changes the load I name the change aloud before correcting it.
I practise identifying the present speaker, then closing my end while Wren is still allowed to say stop. She says it twice to check I mean it.
I put the light screen between the false receiving mark and the ordinary reader. Imani changes the lamp’s angle until she can see without glare.
I rehearse the decoy with an empty line while everyone watches. When it begins using a familiar voice, I close it instead of trying to make the imitation better.

choices.label: Study the names and terms of safe passage

effects.detail: I learned which divine name and office to invoke.

choices.label: Practise the release sequence once more

effects.detail: I used the remaining time to rehearse the release.

beats.text: The guardian’s gaze stops on the marks of my earlier forced crossing. Knowing a name will not make him overlook how I treated the last road. I will need another way to ask.

The lower entrance is inside a disused service building near the waterfront. The building is Voss's invention before it is a place: temporary walls, false measurements, a real electricity supply someone has continued paying for. From the pavement it looks like something waiting to be demolished.
Leila has brought Dennis to hold the outer line. He checks the chair she sets beside the bell case, tests its legs and sits down.
“Four minutes,” he says.
“Only after we connect the reader.”
“Then tell me when you connect the reader.”
She promises. He takes a small battery timer from his pocket. I am glad someone in the room still believes a timer can do its job without developing a second meaning.
Voss opens the inner door with a key. It leads to a staircase which should come out below ground. Instead it descends beside a wall of dark water. A fish passes on the other side, turns, and is gone.
Imani puts her hand on the rail.
“Does that stay there?”
“Usually,” Voss says.
“Try again.”
“It will hold while the outer line remains stable.”
“Better.”

We go down in single file. Miso moves ahead, stopping at every landing to sniff the corner. Wren stays near the back with Julian. She keeps looking at the water and then touching the card in her pocket.
Halfway down, the lights go out behind me.

Nobody speaks. I take out the torch and point it at the steps. The beam catches water running upward along a crack in the concrete. Something knocks against the wall on the other side, three slow impacts.
My body knows the rhythm before I do.
Imani looks back. “Not the flat.”
“I know.”
“Just making sure you know.”

The corridor at the bottom ends in a pair of stone doors. A narrow opening lies between them. Through it, I can see the lights of the lower station and, far above those lights, the upside-down shape of Toronto.
Between me and the opening stands a figure carrying a standard topped by a jackal.

He doesn't look like Anubis. Even before I can decide why, the distinction feels important. His posture is forward, alert, the way a person stands before a race begins. When he turns towards me, the end of the standard scrapes a line through the dust.
“No compelled passage,” he says.
Voss steps forward. “The operator is expecting us.”
The standard comes down between him and the doors.
“I heard the words you chose.”
Voss stops.
I find the page in Mum's notebook. The sketch is rough, but the shape of the standard is unmistakable.
Wepwawet looks at the open book.
“The conservator,” he says. “She asked better questions after the first one.”
“What was the first one?” I ask.
“How to get in without being stopped.”
“What should she have asked?”
“How to bring everyone back.”
I hear Julian draw a breath behind me. Wren moves closer to the wall. The pressure of the waiting voices has changed her shape at the edges; her sleeves look too long even for the borrowed coat.
Wepwawet examines each of us. When he reaches Miso, his eyes stop at the collar.
“That one is under claim.”
“Not by choice,” I say.
“A useful distinction. Not yet a release.”
I think of the circle on the kitchen table. I loosened the collar but didn't remove it. Voss has been quiet for too long.
“Let him go,” I tell him.
“He knows the route. If he runs—”
“Let him go.”
The stone doors shift. The gap narrows by an inch.
Voss looks at the standard, then at the cat. He says a word I don't recognise. Miso folds to the floor as the collar loosens completely.
I kneel beside him. He is breathing. His eyes stay open, fixed on Voss.
“You don't have to come farther,” I say.
He gets up slowly. Walks to the edge of the dust line. Looks through the doors.
“I know.”
He crosses back and stands beside my boot.
The opening stops narrowing.
Wepwawet looks at me. “Now ask.”

I could offer the witness receipt and negotiate passage for every person who wants it. I could invoke the office-name I learned, asking him to open a road without claiming it as mine. I could try to force the doors while they are still apart, though the standard hasn't moved an inch and the water beside me is rising.
Or I could turn back. The upper route remains open. There would still be time to cut the outer bell, but not to reach Nadia first.
I put the torch down so both hands are visible.

choices.label: Negotiate passage and return for every willing traveller

effects.detail: I negotiated passage without claiming the road.

choices.label: Invoke Wepwawet’s office-name from Nadia’s notes

effects.detail: Knowledge of Wepwawet opened a safer way.

choices.label: Force the opening — lose one heart and risk serious injury

effects.detail: I tried to force the road and was injured.
The road takes one of the coat’s return knots.

choices.label: Hold his gaze and state a refusal without surrendering the return

effects.detail: I held the ordinary return open without taking a divine guarantee.

choices.label: Refuse the terms; take the flooded maintenance route

effects.detail: I refused the divine terms and took the dangerous bypass.

beats.text: I can feel which inscription is under strain. I still read Mum’s page twice. Being quick at a task is a particularly efficient way to do it wrong before anyone can stop me.
My knee will not take my full weight. Imani carries the reader while I use the wall. Forcing the earlier crossing has not stayed behind at the doors.

Beyond the doors, the lower station opens around me. It is larger than it was during the first rescue, or I am arriving from a side I didn't see. Rows of switchboards rise towards an arch of dark water. Telephone cables hang between stone columns. Every cable carries a brass label.
The labels are names.
Some are written in letters I recognise. Some use scripts I cannot read. A few are only marks, as if the person writing them had almost forgotten the shape before reaching the end.
Julian stops beside one, not touching it.
“Those aren't all dead callers,” he says.
Leila looks at the label. She recognises the name.
“It's a patient. From the first tests. She declined.”
Voss says nothing.
I turn towards him. “You kept them.”
“I kept the routing information. I didn't send—”
“The line can't tell the difference,” Julian says.

I look down the long rows of names. People waiting for a call. People who refused one. People who once loved someone who used a system that couldn't bear an empty space. The bypass has turned a record into a place to hold them.
Wren presses her hands over her ears.
“They're louder here.”
Imani takes her to the edge of a table, away from the nearest cables. Julian sets up the reader. Leila checks the receiving sequence against the original card. I follow Miso towards the inner room.
Mum is standing this time. She has wrapped a strip of cloth around her hand, but it has burned through in several places.
When she sees me, her face closes with fear before relief can reach it.
“No. {{firstName}}, I told you—”
“I listened. Then we found the other reader.”
“Who came with you?”
I tell her. Her eyes reach Voss before I finish.
He stops in the doorway.
“I have the revised sequence,” he says.
Mum looks at the bag, the brass box, Julian's grey hand. She understands more from those objects than I could have explained.
Then she looks back at me.
“You've been learning.”
“You left notes.”
“Not enough.”
“No.”
She accepts the answer. It costs her something; I can see it. I don't soften it before she has time to hear it.
I take her free hand again. This time I don't need to check whether the familiar rough patch is there. Her thumb closes over mine.
“I wanted to call,” she says.
“I know.”

“No. I need to tell you this part properly. I tried. Then I stopped. Every time I thought I could make the next attempt safer, I found another reason to wait. At first it was the right decision. After a while I couldn't tell how much was right and how much was being afraid to hear you ask me to come home.”
“You could have let me ask.”
“Yes.”
Her voice breaks on the word. I look at the burned cloth around her other hand. I am angry with her and afraid for her at the same time, and neither feeling makes room for the other.
Imani comes to the doorway. “We need to put the reader close enough to connect without pulling the hand control.”
Mum wipes her face with her sleeve. “Under the table. There's a shelf. Don't touch the left bracket.”
The instructions give her a way to stand upright again.

For ten minutes I work around her. Julian positions the reader. Imani passes the connectors in the order I rehearsed. Leila renews the holding marks without closing the release side. Miso moves along the floor, checking where the cables pass into the stone.
Voss stands by the master switch. He has the task he asked for and no private line to operate. I watch him whenever his hands move.
Wren comes in last. Mum looks at her face, then at the card she is holding.
“Hello,” she says.
Wren doesn't answer at once.
“You called me the Unnamed.”
“I didn't know what else to call what I was hearing.”
“Wren.”
Mum nods. “Hello, Wren.”
Wren moves closer. “You kept saying {{firstName}}.”
“I know.”
“I thought I could bring you there.”
Mum looks at me, then down at the cable in her hand. “That was kind. It was also dangerous.”
Wren's mouth twists. “People can do both?”
“Yes,” Mum says. “I'm finding that very inconvenient.”
It is not a grand explanation. Wren seems to prefer it.
Julian checks the reader. The first indicator glows. The second remains dark.
“We need the actual receiving mark,” he says. “Nadia's. The one Adrian copied.”
Mum nods towards the back of the panel. “His version's there. Mine is underneath.”
I kneel and find the two layers. The false signature is visible on top. Beneath it, scratched into the brass, is the mark my mother drew before the bypass existed.
I copy it exactly. The final stroke curves left instead of right. A small error to build eleven months around.
The second indicator comes on.
Leila calls Dennis through the outer line.
“Connected,” she says.
The timer starts.
At first the reader makes no sound. I can hear the click of the outer timer through Leila's phone, the shallow breathing of the people nearest me, and a relay moving under Nadia's table.
Then every label in the room turns towards the brass box.
I am not sure labels can turn. I watch the movement happen anyway, name after name lifting its lower edge as if caught by a wind I cannot feel.
Julian puts his good hand on the lever.
“First stage.”
I close the holding mark.

The resistance is immediate. Not pain, exactly. The sense that a weight has been placed on the far end of a long tool I am trying to keep level. My fingers tighten around the chalk. I remember the torn papers on Julian's desk. The forty-one seconds. The way breathing stopped the pieces shaking.
I breathe.
Wren lays her receiving card beside the reader. Her name appears on the blank indicator strip.
Mum starts to open her burned hand.
A cable jerks through the brass loop around her wrist. She cries out and closes her fingers again.
Julian lowers the lever. “Not yet. Something's still returning the refusal as a yes.”
Voss turns towards the master panel.
I see his hand stop over a switch he hasn't mentioned.
“What does that do?”
“Return cache.”
“Turn it off.”
“If we clear it, we lose the stored calls.”
“Turn it off.”
He looks at Wren. The reader is pulling separate voices out of her shape; faces flicker across her skin, too fast to distinguish. At the centre, the face she chose is trying to hold still.
“Eva's in there somewhere,” he says.
I want to shout. I need the breath to hold the mark.
Imani steps between him and the switch. “You heard her leave.”
Voss takes out the photograph. I hadn't realised he still had it with him. He studies Eva's face as if the answer might be written somewhere the camera failed to focus.
Leila's phone says, “Two minutes.”
Mum loosens one finger. Another cable slams against the table. The receiver count doubles.
Wren looks at me. “Too fast.”

Julian has one hand on the lever and the other held uselessly against his chest. He could slow the release, but not while he holds the reader aligned. Imani could reach him, but that would leave Voss alone at the master panel.
My mark begins to tremble.
Miso puts one paw beside the outer circle. Not inside it. He waits until I nod, then adds his weight to the connection. The trembling eases.
I have seconds in which I can think.

The first option is to finish the separation. It needs a receiver who can remain distinct while the messages move, a route that recognises Wren, and another person to hold the reader steady. I have either earned those things or I haven't. Wanting them now won't put them in the room.

The second is to break the bell. Leila can sever the crossing from outside while Nadia still has enough strength to leave. Wren's new record may hold her shape, but the unfinished voices will be cut away. Some will never reach the people waiting for them.

The third is to take the whole receiving load myself. Not replace Nadia under Voss's old instruction; choose a new, limited service and give the others time to disconnect. I would stay inside. They could build a way to reach me, but nobody here knows how to bring me home.
Mum sees where I am looking.
“You do not owe me that,” she says.
“I know.”
“You need to know before you choose.”

I look at her burned hand, at Julian's bandage, at the card Wren wrote her own name on. I look at Imani, who has been waiting for me to make a decision she can disagree with and still help me carry out.
Leila's phone says, “Ninety seconds.”
I put the chalk against the last open line.

beats.text: I look past him. Three passengers sit under advertisements for things I have never heard of. A woman with a cardboard suitcase is picking loose threads from her gloves. A boy in a school uniform holds a loaf of bread wrapped in a tea towel. Neither looks at me.
“My mother's missing,” I say.
“That is something that happened. What did you leave?”
The doors wait. The woman stops picking her glove.
I could say the flat. The answer is technically true. I could make a joke and see whether the driver has a sense of humour, though he hasn't offered much evidence.
I look down at the chemistry worksheet still stuck to my boot by a strip of wet tape from the alley.
“I stopped putting her things back,” I say. “When my aunt tidied them away. I used to get them out again. Then it was easier not to.”
My voice has gone quieter than I want. I hope Imani won't turn towards me.
The driver reaches for a pad of transfers. “Easier to sleep?”
“Sometimes.”
He stamps the paper and gives it to me.
“Rest isn't charged against you here.”
Miso puts his head out of my coat. “Anubis.”
The driver tips his cap. In the window beside him, his reflection has a long black muzzle and upright ears. I look at the real man, then back at the glass.
“Yes,” he says. “Please keep clear of the doors.”
I sit down with the transfer going damp in my hand. Imani sits beside me. For a whole block she says nothing.
Then she points at my boot.
“Question four's wrong.”
“I know.”
“Just checking.”
I peel the worksheet off. Outside, the streetlights stop at the edge of a wide black river.
Mum pushes me towards the door.
“Go.”
“I'm not leaving you.”
“Then you won't be able to come back.”
Imani drags Julian over the threshold. Miso lands beside them. My mother's hand is still on my coat.
I turn and put my hand over hers. One quick pressure. Then she lets go.
The door shuts against my shoulder.
On the blank wall of the exchange room, I leave a streak of blood from my elbow and a white chalk mark that won't close.

c15_tail.title: The Wrong End of the Rink

beats.text: Afterwards, she takes off her helmet and runs a hand through flattened hair. There is a red mark across her forehead where the padding sat.
“You came.”
“You sent an address.”
“People ignore addresses all the time.”
I think of the notebook and decide not to turn that into an observation.
Her dad goes to fetch the car. She sits beside me and starts undoing the fastening on a shin pad.
“How'd it go?” I ask.
“I don't know. They don't tell you there.”
“You saved that one.”
“I saved several.”
“The one near the end.”
She looks at me. Then she laughs, a quick tired sound.
“Thanks for the detailed analysis.”
I show her Julian's messages. The smile leaves her face, but she doesn't stop undoing the fastening.
“You waited?”
“For once.”
“You can stop making everything a confession. I just asked.”

She pulls the pad free. Under it, her leg is bruised along the shin. I had been thinking of her as the person who arrived carrying a weapon. Looking at the marks, I begin to understand how much work came before she picked it up.

c15_tail~1.title: The Wrong End of the Rink

beats.text: Her dad brings the car around. Imani makes me sit in front because her bag occupies most of the back seat. As her dad drives towards the annex, the heater blows too hot on my wet boots.
“What's wrong with the cat?” her dad asks suddenly.
I look at him.
“The black one. I saw it at the window yesterday. Didn't move for half an hour.”
I consider possible answers. “He's waiting for somebody.”
Her dad nods as if that makes sense.
Outside the annex, he waits until Imani and I reach the door. She turns back and waves. He gives the short two-finger gesture I saw at the rink, then drives away.
Inside, Julian has covered an entire sheet with the same connector drawing. This time he has labelled the missing part.
SECOND READER. INDEPENDENT ACKNOWLEDGEMENT.
I put my notebook beside it.
“Let's go home,” I say. “Properly. All of us.”
I answer before the second ring.
For a moment all I hear is someone breathing too close to a microphone. I am about to ask who it is when the person outside knocks. The breath on the line catches at exactly the same time as mine.
I don't say my name. I learned that much from a school assembly about scams, though the person giving the assembly did not discuss visitors wearing my face.
“{{firstName}}?”
I put the phone on the counter. I want both hands free. I don't know what I expect to do with them.
I hold the power button until the screen goes black. For two seconds the flat is quiet.
Then the phone rings again. The screen stays dark.
I put it on the counter and step away. This feels like the sort of thing that should solve a problem if I do it decisively enough. It doesn't.
The third knock comes from the door.
“{{firstName}}? Please. I know you can hear it.”
I recognise the voice, and that is worse than not recognising it.
Eventually I touch the screen. It lights up with the same call still waiting, as though the phone has simply refused to take part in my decision. I answer without putting it to my ear.
‘I'm going to need help,’ I tell Imani. ‘I don't know what kind yet.’
She looks towards the road. ‘Then don't tell me I have to. Ask.’
I try again. ‘Will you come?’
‘Yes.’ She checks the map on her phone. ‘And I'm telling my dad where we are.’
Miso steps around a puddle. ‘Sensible.’
‘You can carry your own phone when you grow thumbs,’ she tells him.
He looks offended. I leave them to establish their own relationship.
‘Just keep up,’ I say. ‘I'll explain when I can.’
Imani stops.
I get three steps farther before noticing. When I turn, she is still standing by the bins.
‘I'm not your employee,’ she says.
‘I didn't mean—’
‘Then use different words.’
I look at the map on my phone. I don't know whether the next street is the safe one. She doesn't either. That is not a reason to pretend she agreed to be instructed.
‘Will you come to the annex?’ I ask.
She considers it. ‘Your aunt asked me to check on you. I'm doing that. We'll see after.’
She walks beside me, leaving more space than before.
‘Tell me what the transfer gives you before I pay,’ I say.
The driver's hand remains open. ‘A record that you entered this road willingly. No claim on your return. No permission to speak for you.’
‘And you keep what I say?’
‘Only the account needed for the crossing.’
I think about it, then tell him I left a kitchen where my mother's things have begun to look like somebody else's clutter. I don't give him every memory attached to that sentence.
He stamps the transfer and gives it to me. ‘Defined terms,’ he says. ‘A useful habit.’
Imani puts her fare away. ‘We're keeping that habit.’
We sit down together. Miso climbs out of my collar, dislodging a considerable amount of fur onto my coat.
‘Nothing,’ I say. ‘I haven't left anything.’
In the window, my reflection smiles. I haven't moved my mouth.
The driver closes his hand. ‘Then I cannot issue the transfer.’
The doors remain open. Beyond them, the staircase is visible. I can get there, but it will not count as a witnessed crossing.
I feel a moment of triumph, followed by the uncomfortable recognition that I have won nothing except permission to leave without the thing I need.
Imani steps down first. She does not look at me until both feet are on the concrete.
‘Was that worth it?’
‘I don't know yet.’
‘Next time, work that out before.’
Miso follows, saying nothing at all.
I try to push past the driver's arm.
I do not get far. The space beyond the fare reader lengthens while my feet stay where they are. My elbow strikes the rail hard enough to make my fingers numb.
The driver has not moved.
‘You may refuse passage,’ he says. ‘You may not turn everyone else's road into your entrance.’
Imani takes my good arm and pulls me back. I let her. The shame comes before the pain, which is an unpleasant order for either feeling.
At the next ordinary landing, the doors open. No transfer. No blessing. A way out which remains a way out because he said it would.
On the concrete, I unwrap the dressing at my elbow and see fresh blood. Imani has stopped asking whether it hurts.
‘I don't want to give you that,’ I say.
The driver inclines his head. ‘Then use the exit.’
I expected an argument. Getting none makes me hesitate.
Imani steps down beside me. Miso follows. The streetcar remains until I am clear of the doors, then moves away across the river.
‘We still reach the exchange room?’ I ask.
‘We walk farther,’ Miso says. ‘Not every refusal ends the road.’

The steps are steep and my boots are wet. I spend the climb thinking about the question I chose not to answer. I don't decide whether I should have answered it. I am glad the decision was allowed to remain mine.
I show Imani the back of the photograph before putting the notebook away.
‘Those were under Eva's name,’ I say. ‘I copied the crossed-out one too.’
She takes a picture of my page, discovers the photograph comes out blank, and writes the numbers into her own notebook instead.
‘Two copies,’ she says. ‘If one of us drops something off another roof.’
‘We haven't been on a roof.’
‘Give it time.’
I laugh. When the fear returns, I don't have to carry the information alone with it.
I close the notebook before Imani can see the back of the photograph.
‘Anything else he gave you?’ she asks.
‘No.’
The word comes easily. I tell myself I am checking the numbers before worrying anyone. I tell myself I will share them when they make sense.
Imani watches me put the notebook away.
‘Okay,’ she says.
I had wanted the lie to end the question. It does. That is not as reassuring as I expected.
I slide the evidence across the desk.
Thoth gives me a receipt with a clear list of what he is retaining. I check the recorder's serial number, though I have never cared about a serial number in my life. Julian checks it too.
‘Copies remain yours,’ Thoth says. ‘The correction will show both the false entry and the evidence against it.’
I nod. I am not buying the disappearance of a bad fact. I am making it possible for someone else to see what happened.
I grab the open book.
It shuts before I can lift it. My sleeve is caught between the covers. The third pen stops above the page, perfectly still.
Thoth looks at my hand.
‘You came to challenge a stolen authority.’
I let go. The sleeve comes free with a neat tear along the seam.
Julian has gone pale. Imani steps back from the desk. I cannot think of an answer that makes the last five seconds look better.
Thoth copies the public route reference onto a card and puts it beyond my reach. ‘You may take the address. You may not use my witness seal.’
I take the card only after he nods. The walk to the stairs feels very long.
‘I'm keeping the recorder,’ I say.
Thoth withdraws the evidence form. ‘Then I cannot certify the correction.’
‘Can you give us the address?’
He considers the reference number, then writes a public routing entry on a card. ‘A destination. Not proof of your authority to change what happens there.’
I take it. My mother's voice remains in my pocket. The witness receipt stays on his desk.
Julian does not tell me that I chose badly. He asks me to put the difference in the notebook so nobody later assumes I have something I don't.
I grab Julian's sleeve and pull.
He comes away from the panel with a sharp cry. His hand has gone grey to the wrist. I get his good arm over my shoulder and take his weight before my injured elbow can object.
Behind him, the spare connector remains in the socket. I see it. I know it might have helped. I keep moving.
Julian tries to say my name. I tell him to save the breath until he is through the door.
Imani takes his other side. Together we get him over the threshold.
I reach for the spare connector.
The metal is hot enough to burn through my glove. I pull it free and fall against the panel. Behind me, Imani swears and hauls Julian away from the closing contact.
‘{{firstName}}!’
I turn. His injured hand hangs at a wrong, stiff angle. She has his good arm over her shoulder, carrying a weight I chose not to reach first.
I help them through the door with the connector burning in my pocket. It may be useful. It doesn't make Imani meet my eyes.
Julian says, ‘You got it, then,’ in a voice I cannot read.
I put the phone away.
For the rest of the session I watch the puck closely enough to lose it twice. I don't understand every decision Imani makes, but I begin to recognise when she's pleased with one.
When she looks towards the benches again, I am still there.
The archive message can wait until the whistle. I don't pretend waiting was easy. It matters that I chose it anyway.
I show Imani's dad the message and say I need to go. He nods, distracted by a shot at the far end of the rink.

Outside, I call Leila before going to the flat. She meets me there. Together we find the manual before Imani's session finishes. It is a useful hour. I keep telling myself that while looking at my phone.
Imani's message arrives at eleven thirty: “Went looking for you. Dad said you had another thing.”
I start an explanation, delete half of it and send the plain version: I left to find the manual. Should've told you myself.
Her reply comes several minutes later. Yes.
When she joins me at the flat, she asks to read the diagram before agreeing to the next part of the plan.
‘You don't have to keep us here,’ I tell the girl. ‘What happens if we leave?’
She looks at the door. ‘He asks why I let you.’
‘You can say we asked you.’
‘That won't be enough.’
I don't tell her it will. Instead I ask whether she wants to come as far as the window and see the roof herself.
She moves aside. Only a little. Enough to let Imani reach the catch without pushing past her.
‘Just looking,’ she says.
‘Just looking,’ I agree.
‘Voss said to let us take the reader,’ I say. ‘It's part of the test.’
The girl's face brightens with relief. Then it tightens.
‘He would have told me.’
I point towards the door. ‘Ask him.’
She turns for long enough that Imani can reach the window. I have bought a few seconds by making another person doubt what she was told.
When the girl turns back, she knows. I can see it before she speaks.
‘You do that too,’ she says.
The cable nearest my boot coils tightly enough to crack the floor tile.
I swing the torch towards her hand, trying to knock the cable away.
It goes through her wrist. The force of my own movement pulls me off balance. I hit the cupboard hard with my injured elbow.
The girl looks down at the place I tried to strike. Her face becomes my mother's for one terrible second.
‘Don't,’ Imani says. I'm not sure which of us she means.
I get up. The torch has broken against the wood. The girl steps back from me, opening a path without offering trust.
Outside the door, Voss begins turning the handle.
‘We're taking the reader,’ I say. ‘I'm not making a deal about my mother.’
The girl watches me. ‘I wasn't asking for her.’
I look at the cable in her hand and realise I heard a threat before she made one.
‘Then let us leave.’
She steps away from the window. ‘You can. I don't have to like it.’
Imani opens the catch. Cold air moves through the room. I keep watching the girl's face, expecting another borrowed one. It stays her own unfinished shape.
For once, nobody makes the refusal mean more than it does.
I offer the witness papers with my hands open.
‘Passage for those who choose it. Return for the same people, if they choose to leave. No replacement required.’
Wepwawet examines the receiving record. He looks at Wren, not at me.
‘Your choice?’
‘Mine,’ she says.
The standard lifts. The stone doors part far enough for the equipment bag.
‘The road is open,’ he says. ‘Keep the terms you named.’
I step through without trying to take a piece of the opening with me.
‘Wepwawet,’ I say, carefully. ‘Opener of the Ways. I ask for a road, not control of it.’
His shadow moves before he does. For a moment the jackal on the standard seems larger than the room.
‘You know which work you are asking for.’
I show him the page in Nadia's notebook. He reads the little correction beside the sketch.
‘She learned.’
‘So are we.’
He turns the standard aside. The gap widens. Knowledge has not made him mine to command; it has let me make a request he can recognise.
Wren goes through beside me, holding her card in one hand.
I push towards the opening.
The standard strikes the floor. The sound knocks the breath from my lungs. I land on my knees, skin burning where the stone scrapes through my jeans.
Wepwawet has not struck me. He has stopped the road moving with me on it. The distinction does not improve the pain.
Imani puts the equipment bag down before helping me stand.
‘You have a route back,’ the god says. ‘Take it if you will not ask for passage.’
I look at the blood on my knee, then at the person holding the door.
‘Passage,’ I say. The word is difficult to get out. ‘For everyone who chooses it.’
He waits until I have named the return terms too. Only then does the opening widen.
I refuse the terms and take the upper stair with the others. Wepwawet does not stop me.

Miso finds an old maintenance return halfway up, a route Adrian once used before the stone doors were installed. It is narrow, flooded and no longer held level. I can reach the lower station, but I won't arrive on a recognised road.

The first section is almost ordinary. Then the water rises to my knees. Imani carries the reader above her head while Julian keeps the receiving card dry inside his coat. I use two holding marks to cross a place where the floor has gone. One collapses before I finish. I strike my knee against a submerged step and keep moving because stopping would leave the person behind me without a place to put their foot.

At the lower end, Miso opens a service panel. I climb into the station soaked, late and unwitnessed. I did not have to accept the god's terms. I have paid for the other road with time and a knee that will not take my full weight.
Imani puts the reader down carefully. “We do not pretend that was free,” she says. I nod before trying to stand.

I ask another question. Wren looks at the empty glove on the floor. “I heard you,” she says. “I said not yet.” I begin to explain the deadline. Imani sets the cracker packet down hard enough that I stop. Nobody has to shout for the room to become uncomfortable. I back away from the question, but Wren keeps watching my hands for the rest of the test.
I put the tested clay figures along the reader’s supports. Each carries one defined segment, then stops. The rehearsal gives me a way to share a load nobody could safely hold alone.
I fit the spare connector into the reader’s empty brace. The component I took gives the load another point of support. Julian checks it carefully before trusting his injured hand near it.
“Clear it,” I tell Voss. “Then leave the switch.”
He doesn't move.
Wren turns towards him. For a moment she is Eva, exactly as she stood in the photograph. I see Voss's whole body lean forward.
Then Wren returns to her own face.
“I could keep doing that,” she says. “Would you ever stop asking?”
He looks at the photograph. At the master panel. At Nadia, trying not to cry out while another cable pulls against her hand.
At last he opens the cache switch.
The photograph tears across its folded crease. He catches both halves and holds them together, although the picture no longer lines up.
The count on the reader drops.
“Imani,” I say.

She moves towards the reader, then stops where I need her. The support comes from the work I prepared and the person still willing to hold the other end. Voss stays where Dennis's voice through the phone tells him to stay. It is an arrangement nobody would have believed possible two days ago.
I open the release side of the mark.

The first voice is a man's. He asks whether his brother collected the tools from the shed. It is so ordinary I almost laugh. Wren looks at the label turning towards her, then at the receiving indicator. A light flashes. The man says thank you, impatiently, as if everyone has taken too long about a simple errand.
His label falls flat.

A second voice follows. Then four. Then enough that I can't separate the words. Wren can. I can see the work in the way she holds her shoulders, the careful pauses between one acknowledgement and the next.
Mum's hand begins to open.
Leila reaches her first. She doesn't pull. She slides a clean piece of cloth under the burned palm and supports the wrist while the cable loosens.
Nadia looks at her sister.
“I'm sorry.”
“Later,” Leila says. Her voice is shaking. “Do that later.”
Mum laughs once and starts crying. The brass loop opens. Her hand comes free.
For a second I nearly let go of the chalk.
Imani says my name sharply. I breathe and hold the mark.
Wren is fading at the edges. Her card remains solid on the table, a small plain rectangle amid the moving light.
“Where do you want to stand?” I ask her.
She looks at the doorway. At the strip of lake visible beyond it. At Miso's paw beside my chalk circle.
“Here. For now.”
“Then keep that.”
She presses one hand to the card. Her face steadies.
A woman speaks through the reader. I recognise Mrs. Bell's voice before the name turns towards me. She does not ask about a pharmacy this time.
“Martin,” she says.
The letter in my notebook grows warm. Somewhere far above me, a receiving line opens for one message. I don't hear the rest. It isn't addressed to me.
The completed address in my notebook grows warm. Martin has already received his letter. I hear Celia’s name once, then give her call room to finish without me.
Miso lifts his paw. I hold the connection alone for the last few seconds.
The final voice is very quiet. A girl says, “You can put it down now.”
Voss closes his eyes. He doesn't answer. He doesn't reach for a switch. He folds the two halves of the photograph together and lowers his hands.
Julian releases the lever.
Nothing rings.
The labels settle. The cables hang loose. The weight at the far end of my mark lifts so suddenly that I fall onto one knee.
Imani catches the chalk before it rolls under the table.
“Done?” she asks Julian.
He checks the indicator, then checks it again because he doesn't trust a first answer anymore.
“Done.”
Wren stands beside the reader with her hands on the table. She is still there. Her coat is too big. One glove is missing. Her face is hers.
Mum takes a step towards me and almost falls. Leila catches her under one arm. I take the other side, feeling the weight of her ordinary body for the first time since she disappeared.

Miso heads for the stairs without waiting to be told. Wren picks her card up carefully and follows him. Julian carries the reader with both hands; his grey fingers have begun to take colour around the knuckles.
Voss remains beside the master panel.
“Adrian,” Leila says.
He looks up.
“You're coming out too.”
He nods. Picks up the empty equipment bag. Follows.
At the staircase, Mum stops to look back once. I let her. Then I put my hand over hers and help her towards the light.
I asked Thoth for one lesson after this, in a room with an ordinary exit. I still mean to go. Accepting the lesson has not forgiven the years he missed, and he has finally stopped confusing the two.
Thoth’s letter is folded beside the notebook. I have not answered it. Mum asks whether I want it put away. “Leave it there,” I say. I want deciding to take longer than one frightened weekend.

At the top of the stairs, Dennis gives Mum a blanket before he asks her name. She holds it around her shoulders with the good hand and looks at the ordinary wall behind her as if she can't believe it has stopped being a doorway.
Leila phones for an ambulance. This part she knows how to do. She gives the location, the injuries, the number of people who need assessment. She does not start with the impossible explanation.

Voss sits on a low concrete step. When the police arrive, he gets up without being asked. Leila tells them he has information about Nadia's disappearance and unsafe equipment in two buildings. There will be time later to work out which words can fit in a statement. For now, she gives names and addresses and makes sure they are written down.
Imani phones her dad.

I hear her say, “I'm safe,” then, “I know,” then, “I can't explain all of it over the phone.” She keeps the call going until he reaches her. When he arrives, he hugs her so tightly her feet move off the ground.
The private cadence in the register stays off every recording. When Mum uses my name across a room, she uses {{firstName}}. It is the name I turn towards.
Mum watches them. I stand beside her, close enough that my sleeve touches the blanket.
“You can do that,” I say.
She looks at me, uncertain for the first time in a way that has nothing to do with the machinery.
I move first. She wraps the blanket around both of us. Her shoulder is thinner than I remember. I press my face into it and finally stop keeping track of who is watching.
At the hospital, the receptionist asks whether Nadia has identification. Leila produces a folder. Of course she brought a folder. I begin laughing and can't stop until it turns into something else.
Wren waits with Imani in a row of plastic chairs. A nurse asks whether she is family. Wren looks at the card in her hand, then at me.
“Yes,” I say, and then stop before deciding for her. “If she wants.”
Wren thinks about it. “I can wait.”
The nurse gives her a visitor sticker. Wren spends the next hour peeling one corner up and pressing it down again, fascinated by how it stays when she chooses not to hold it.

Julian's hand has regained most of its colour. He still can't bend two fingers properly. Leila makes sure somebody examines them rather than accepting that magical damage must require magical neglect.
Miso stays outside the hospital doors. I find him under a bench when I come out for air. His bare neck looks strangely small without the collar.
“Where will you go?” I ask.
He looks at me. Then at the hospital entrance.
“Where's the clean shirt?”
I sit on the bench. The sun has risen. I missed the moment it happened.

My phone is full of ordinary notifications: school messages, a discount code, somebody replying to a group chat that has carried on without knowing anything about my weekend. I read each one because I can.
Under them is a new draft call. No number. No caller ID.
The destination is Friday, 02:13.
I don't press it yet. I take the phone inside, where Mum can see it too.
When Imani talks about selection, she reminds me she looked for me after the first session. I listen before offering to come to the next one.
Mum borrows a pen from the nurse and draws the return circuit on the back of a hospital menu. The soup choices get in the way. She works around them.
“The first connection kept a route back to where the claim began. It couldn't close while the receiving instruction was still active.”
“You're saying I called myself.”
“I'm saying you can. I don't know whether you have to.”
The distinction feels like something I learned on the stairs: an open road doesn't decide whether I use it.
I look at the draft call. Friday, 02:13. My kitchen. The chair at the table. The version of me who hasn't yet learned which details will become important.

I could tell myself everything. The bell, the notebook, the false signature. I try to imagine receiving that list from an unknown caller and remember how close I came to turning the phone off. Maybe a message can only carry what the person on the other end can hold.
Mum hands back the phone. She doesn't tell me what to choose.

Dennis gives me the scores from the match he missed. I bring him a printout and stay while he points out which child is his grandson. The return line cost him a Saturday. It is a small enough debt to remember without turning it into a legend.

Julian and I finish the crossing report before its end date. If I cannot leave the station, he takes my recorded account. The divine office gets the reader or a written account of why we still need it. Anubis sends back a receipt, not a new obligation.
The counter-ledger stays in the archive, available to families challenging the calls they refused. I do not get to decide which of them will use it.

Mum and I close every copy of my private cadence that the station could still reach. Wren listens only as long as she agrees to. I broke one promise about that name; repairing the damage does not make her pretend I kept it.
The return log has all our signatures, including Dennis’s. Nobody can renew the agreement by copying his yes. We file its completed end beside the beginning.

The counter-ledger comes back with scorch marks on its cover. The entries are intact. Julian catalogues the original and the copy separately, so nobody can mistake the correction for the thing it corrected.
I call.
For one ring I hear nothing. Then the line opens to the sound of my own frightened breathing.
I press my free hand against the hospital chair.
“Whatever happens,” I say, “do not open the door.”
At the other end, a chair scrapes across laminate.
“How do I stop it?”
My own voice, younger by two days and a great deal else.
“Blue notebook. Kitchen drawer.”
“What?”
“Mum's notebook. Get it. And {{firstName}}—”
The connection closes.
I sit with the phone still against my ear. Mum's good hand rests on my sleeve.
“What were you going to say?” she asks.
I look at the hospital menu with its impossible diagram. The floor outside the curtain. My aunt returning with tea she will insist somebody drinks before it gets cold.
“I don't know. Something useful.”
Mum rubs her thumb across the worn bird patch on my coat.
“You got the notebook,” she says.

Three weeks later, the flat contains more people than it has chairs. Julian brings a folding one from the archive, which he says should not leave the building and has therefore labelled with the building's name in case that helps.

Leila makes dinner. Mum tries to help and is told to sit down. They argue for four minutes about whether chopping one onion counts as rest. I let them. I hadn't realised I missed being annoyed by both of them at once.

Voss is under investigation. There are statements about Nadia's disappearance, equipment records, unsafe access and financial arrangements nobody in my kitchen is qualified to explain. His wife has asked for the original recording of Eva's call. Julian sends a copy through a solicitor. I don't hear what she says when she receives it. I don't need to.

Mum goes to appointments. Some days her hand hurts too much to hold a pen. Some nights she knocks on my bedroom door to make sure I'm there, then pretends she needed to borrow a charger. I stop pretending to believe her and let her sit for a while.

Leila and I do not repair everything in one conversation. She starts telling me when she doesn't know something. I start telling her before leaving the building. It is inconvenient for both of us. We keep doing it.

Wren has been living in the annex's spare room while people work out what papers the ordinary world will accept. She comes over wearing a coat that fits. She has learned to dislike olives and asks whether this is a personality or just a food opinion.
“Both, if you mention it often enough,” Imani tells her.

Julian has called his sister. He didn't get the wedding back. He told her why the photographs had become homework. I don't know how much she believed. I know he is going to her house on Sunday and bringing a cake he has been instructed not to choose himself.
Miso sleeps on my chemistry textbook. I move him only when absolutely necessary, which he defines differently from me.
After dinner, Imani stays to help clear the table. Her phone lights up with a message from the selection coach. She reads it twice, then hands me the screen without speaking.
I read the message. Look at her. She is trying very hard not to smile before I do.
“You got it.”
“Conditional. Still training.”
“You got it.”
She grins properly then. I shout for Leila, who comes in carrying a wet plate and complains that I frightened her before joining the celebration.

Later, when everyone has gone, I find a small paper bird on the fire escape. Wren made it from the blank end of an old archive form. Its wings are uneven. I bring it inside and put it beside Mum's blue notebook.
My phone rings.
Imani. She left her gloves under the chair, and she would like I to stop telling people she cried at the message, because she didn't.
I look towards the kitchen, where Mum is trying to make toast without setting off the alarm.
I answer.
THE END
“Leila. Tell Dennis.”
She looks at the reader, then at Nadia's hand. I see her understand the whole choice before she speaks into the phone.
“Sever the outer circuit. On my count.”
Wren takes one step away from the table.
“Will it hurt?”
“I don't know,” I say.
It is the hardest answer I have given her.
Imani goes to her side. “You can hold my hand if you want.”
Wren nods. The borrowed faces move more slowly across her skin, as if the voices are listening too.
Julian makes sure the second reader is detached from the main line. His good hand is precise. His injured one shakes.
Mum opens two fingers. The cable jerks. I add the last of the chalk to the holding mark and press the point down hard enough to hurt.
“Now,” I say.
Through Leila's phone comes a sharp metal crack.
Nothing happens for half a second. Then every label in the room lifts at once.

The sound is not a scream. It is thousands of unfinished syllables cut short, words losing their ends. A request, an apology, somebody asking where a book has been put. I hear fragments and understand none of them well enough to keep.
Mum's cable goes slack.
Leila pulls the brass loop open with both hands. Nadia cries out. I turn towards her and miss the moment Wren falls.
Imani catches her before she reaches the floor. Wren's face has gone pale and difficult to see. Her receiving card lies on the table. I pick it up and put it in her hand.
“Wren.”
She doesn't answer.
I say it again, not as an order, just as the name I know belongs to the person in front of me.
Her fingers close over the card.
For several seconds, all of us wait. I can hear Mum breathing behind me, uneven and too fast. Julian has put the reader down to kneel beside Imani. Miso stands at Wren's feet, his back arched.
Then Wren opens her eyes.
“Quiet,” she says.
Nobody tries to tell her that's good.

The station begins to change. Without the connections holding its different parts together, the rooms no longer fit. The doorway to Nadia's table becomes a narrow arch. The far switchboard slides towards a wall which wasn't there before.
“We leave,” Julian says.

He doesn't wait for agreement. He lifts the reader, checks that Imani has Wren, and moves towards the stairs. I help Leila support Nadia. Miso leads, stopping whenever the floor changes under his paws.
Voss stands alone beside the master panel. The switches have gone dark. He is pressing one with the end of his thumb, over and over, without enough force to move it.
“Come on,” I tell him.
He doesn't hear me. Or he does and doesn't know what to do with the words.
I go back far enough to take his sleeve.
“We're leaving.”
He looks down at my hand. Then at the empty panel. He comes without resisting.

On the first landing, the wall of water moves inward. I feel cold drops on my face. Imani shifts Wren's arm higher across her shoulders and keeps climbing. Julian goes backwards up two steps so he can guide her feet.
The lower station folds away beneath me.
I don't watch it go. My mother is heavy against my side, and every time she breathes I can feel her ribs move through the coat.
At the top, Dennis stands beside a bell broken into two uneven pieces. The button has rolled under his chair.
He looks at the people coming through the door and counts silently. I see his lips move.
“All out?” he asks.
Leila looks back at the narrowing stair.
“All of us,” she says.
It is accurate. I hear the part it leaves out.
I asked Thoth for one lesson after this, in a room with an ordinary exit. I still mean to go. Accepting the lesson has not forgiven the years he missed, and he has finally stopped confusing the two.
Thoth’s letter is folded beside the notebook. I have not answered it. Mum asks whether I want it put away. “Leave it there,” I say. I want deciding to take longer than one frightened weekend.
For the first hour, Wren cannot bear to have anyone speak behind her. She turns at every sound, checking that it comes from a single mouth.
Imani sits where she can be seen. Julian brings water. Leila checks Nadia's burns, then Wren's hands, though there are no marks she knows how to treat.
Voss asks whether he can speak to Wren. She says no. He sits on the far side of the service room until the police come.

I tell them which buildings to check. Leila gives the statements she can make without guessing. Dennis shows them the broken bell. I keep thinking of the names in the lower station, trying to remember more than fragments.

At the hospital, Mum falls asleep halfway through asking a question. I sit beside the bed with her good hand between both of mine. When a nurse needs to check her blood pressure, I stand up too quickly and nearly fall.
“Eat something,” the nurse says.
I want to tell her that food isn't going to address the situation. Then I remember Leila has been saying similar things for eleven months, and I go to find a sandwich.
The private cadence in the register stays off every recording. When Mum uses my name across a room, she uses {{firstName}}. It is the name I turn towards.
Wren is sitting by the window. She has removed the visitor sticker because the name field was blank. Julian gives her a pen. She writes WREN in large careful letters and puts the sticker back.
“Are they gone?” she asks.
“The messages?”
She nods.
“I don't know where they went.”
“You can say you don't know without looking like you're asking me to fix it.”
I sit down at the other end of the row. Outside, a hospital shuttle waits with its engine running.
“I keep trying to remember the names.”
Wren looks out of the window. “I remember some.”
“Can we write them down?”
“Later.”
“Okay.”
I sit without asking again.

When Imani's dad arrives, she goes to him at once. I watch them through the glass panel in the corridor door. She is speaking quickly, trying to explain enough. He listens with one hand on the back of her head.
Mum wakes in the afternoon. She asks for me, then for Leila, then whether everyone got out. I give her the answer Dennis got.
“All of us.”
She closes her eyes. “That's not a small thing.”
“I know.”
I do know. I also know why it doesn't feel like enough.
On my phone, the last unknown call has vanished from the log. In its place is an unsent return connection. The destination is Friday, 02:13.
I show it to Mum. She studies the screen for a long time.
“The bell's gone,” I say.
“The route was made before it broke,” she says. “One message. If you want.”
I look at her, lying in a hospital bed in Toronto. Alive. I look at the numberless call and think about what I could have said to the person I was two days ago.

I take the unsent call into an empty part of the corridor. The hospital is beginning its evening routine. Visitors put on coats. Staff change shifts. Somebody wheels a cart past me and says excuse me twice before I notice I'm in the way.
I sit down where I can see Mum's curtain.

The destination waits on the screen. Friday, 02:13. I remember what the voice said. I remember the terror of hearing myself from a day that hadn't arrived. The reserved date on the line was never the date of the speaker. It was the next place the old receiving instruction could put a message.
Now I can give it the voice it was waiting for.
“Whatever happens,” I say when the call connects, “do not open the door.”
I hear myself move in the kitchen. I give the instruction about the notebook. I start to say one more thing, and the line ends.

Dennis gives me the scores from the match he missed. I bring him a printout and stay while he points out which child is his grandson. The return line cost him a Saturday. It is a small enough debt to remember without turning it into a legend.

Julian and I finish the crossing report before its end date. If I cannot leave the station, he takes my recorded account. The divine office gets the reader or a written account of why we still need it. Anubis sends back a receipt, not a new obligation.
The counter-ledger stays in the archive, available to families challenging the calls they refused. I do not get to decide which of them will use it.

Mum and I close every copy of my private cadence that the station could still reach. Wren listens only as long as she agrees to. I broke one promise about that name; repairing the damage does not make her pretend I kept it.
The return log has all our signatures, including Dennis’s. Nobody can renew the agreement by copying his yes. We file its completed end beside the beginning.

The counter-ledger comes back with scorch marks on its cover. The entries are intact. Julian catalogues the original and the copy separately, so nobody can mistake the correction for the thing it corrected.
For a long time I look at the dark screen.

I want to believe the warning could make the ending different. That another version of me could find one more piece, persuade one more person, hold the chalk a little steadier. I cannot send a second call. The socket is closed.
I go back to Mum.

Three weeks later, Wren and I sit in the annex with a stack of blank cards. She names the voices she remembers. I write them down. Sometimes she knows a whole name and a sentence. Sometimes only a sound. I leave spaces instead of filling them with guesses.

The letter from Mrs. Bell lies beside the cards. Its address has faded but remains legible where Imani copied it. Whether I deliver it or keep it waiting is a decision the broken bell can no longer make for me.
Celia Bell’s address is copied on the first card. I delivered her letter before the bell broke. I mark that promise complete and leave room for the ones we could not finish.
Mum comes to help when her hand allows it. She is home now. The phrase still catches me by surprise. I hear her drop a spoon in the kitchen and feel relief before irritation can reach the sound.

Her return does not arrive as one clean happy thing. There are appointments, police interviews, questions from school and neighbours. She tires quickly. I get angry over small things because the large ones are hard to begin. Once I snap at her for moving my notebook, and she puts it back without telling me how lucky I am to have her there. Later, I apologise for the way I said it. I don't apologise for needing my things left alone.

Leila has started using a shared calendar. She calls it practical. I suspect it is also her way of letting me see the plans before they become instructions. I put my own appointments in, reluctantly. Neither of us celebrates this development out loud.

Wren is quieter than she was before the bell broke. She no longer changes faces when she is frightened. Instead she goes very still and asks people to stop talking for a minute. Usually they do. She is learning which people need reminding.

Julian's hand is recovering. He has told his sister about the wedding memory. She sent him a voice message three minutes long, mostly calling him an idiot and asking when he was coming round. He keeps it backed up in three places.
Imani has a decision from the selection coach. She tells me in person. I go to her next session and sit at the right end of the rink this time, where she can see me without turning her head too far.

Voss does not come to the annex. His part in Nadia's disappearance and the dangerous equipment is being investigated. I don't know whether any ordinary court can account for the rest. I know Leila gave them every record she could explain, including her own signature on the early tests.
One evening, Wren stops halfway through a name.
“What if I forget?” she asks.
I look at the cards. At the spaces I left.
“We'll keep what we've got.”
She nods, but she isn't entirely reassured. I don't add a prettier sentence to make myself feel more helpful.
At home, Mum has burned the toast. The alarm is going off. Miso is shouting from the windowsill as if he has personally discovered a fire nobody else has noticed.
I open the kitchen window. Cold air enters. The alarm stops.
Mum stands in the middle of the room holding a plate with two black rectangles on it.
“I'm out of practice.”
“You were never good at toast.”
She looks offended for a second, then laughs. I put the plate in the sink and get out the cereal.
My phone rings. A schoolfriend, asking whether I want the notes from chemistry. I look at Mum. She nods towards it and goes to fill the kettle.
I answer.
THE END
I ask Julian to describe the choice one more time.
He looks at Mum. At Leila. At Imani, who has gone very still.
“One receiver,” he says. “No forced continuation. We disconnect every other claim. The station becomes a place you operate, not a place that owns everyone attached to it.”
“Can you reach it from outside?”
“Yes. With the second reader.”
“Can you get me out?”
He doesn't look away.
“I don't know.”
Mum says my name. I turn towards her. She is trying to let go of the cable, trying to make the other choice possible before I finish considering this one.
“Don't do it because you're my child,” she says.
I kneel beside the panel. I could still break the bell. That choice remains. The thought helps me keep the next words steady.
“I'm not taking the old instruction.”
Julian lowers the lever enough to open a blank receiving line.
I take the brass feather from the box. Mum's fingers close around my wrist.
For a moment I stay like that, neither pulling away nor giving in. Her hand is warm above the burned cloth. I want another hour in the kitchen. I want her to complain about my hair again.
“I need you to keep looking,” I tell her.
She closes her eyes. When she opens them, there is no agreement in her face. There is understanding, which is different and harder to accept.
“I will.”

I write my name beside the new receiving slot. Then I say what I accept, as carefully as Leila taught me to define a connection. Only the waiting messages. No authority over their senders. No new compulsory calls. A line that can be reached from outside without placing the caller under claim.
The feather warms in my hand.
Julian records each condition. Wren repeats it, listening for a response the rest of us cannot distinguish. Imani checks the page before letting me move to the next line.
The indicator shows my name.
I close the holding mark around myself.
The load arrives slowly enough for me to know I could still stop before the second stage. I say that aloud. Julian confirms it. I take one more breath.
“Continue.”
Mum's hand comes free.

She folds to the floor. Leila catches her. I want to go to them, but the room has changed its sense of distance. The table is near and also impossibly far away. I can hear a woman asking for her son. A boy wants to know whether his bread is still warm. An old man is angry about a set of tools.
I say wait, and the voices wait. Not forever. Long enough for me to understand the difference.
Julian disconnects the old receiving loop. Wren takes her card from the table. Her face steadies as the borrowed voices move towards me instead.
Imani comes close enough that I can see the worn tape on the spare stick she brought from home.
“You don't get to turn into a job,” she says.
“I'll try not to.”
“No. Pick something ordinary. Something we can ask you about.”
I look around the room. There is a chair near the switchboard, its seat split along one seam.
“The chair's terrible.”
She nods, furious and crying now. “We'll start with that.”
Miso stays beside my chalk mark. Leila tells him to come. He looks at her and lies down.
“Miso,” I say.
He puts his head on his paws. “I'm not under claim.”
I cannot make him leave without contradicting the whole connection I just made.
Mum reaches me one last time. I am not sure whether she crossed the room or the room allowed her. She puts her uninjured hand against my cheek.
“I am going to be very difficult about this,” she says.
I laugh. It hurts. “I know.”

Then Leila takes her towards the stairs. Julian carries the reader. Wren stops in the doorway and raises her hand. Imani follows last, looking back until the angle of the corridor takes me out of sight.
The station settles. It is smaller now. No borrowed corridors. No locked inner room. Just the table, the switchboard, the chair and a cat who has chosen to remain.
I sit down. The split seam catches my coat.
At the first socket, a light comes on.
I check the receiving conditions before lifting the handset.
“Hello,” I say. “You can leave a message. You don't have to stay.”
I asked Thoth for one lesson after this, in a room with an ordinary exit. I still mean to go. Accepting the lesson has not forgiven the years he missed, and he has finally stopped confusing the two.
Thoth’s letter is folded beside the notebook. I have not answered it. Mum asks whether I want it put away. “Leave it there,” I say. I want deciding to take longer than one frightened weekend.
I begin by trying to answer every light. Within an hour, I understand why Mum made lists.

Some people want a message carried. Some want to know why they were called. Some have been waiting so long they are angry before I speak. I tell each one what the line can do. I don't promise a receiver will answer.
Miso finds a cupboard with a dry blanket inside and carries it to the foot of my chair. He spends a long time arranging it, then lies down on the bare floor beside it.
“You could use that,” I tell him.
“So could you.”
I pull it over my knees. The station is cold when nobody is moving through it.
At noon, the second reader opens a controlled line from the annex. Julian is on the other end. I can hear him testing the connection by reading out the time, then a list of objects on his desk.
“Can you hear all that?”
“Yes.”
“Good. Don't answer when it's just the test tone.”
“I have learned one or two things.”
“I'm writing them down anyway.”
The private cadence in the register stays off every recording. When Mum uses my name across a room, she uses {{firstName}}. It is the name I turn towards.
Mum comes on after him. She is in hospital. I can hear the soft bleep of a monitor and Leila talking to someone farther away.
“Have you eaten?” she asks.
I look around the station. I'm not hungry. I don't know whether that is reassuring.
“I need to find out how that works here.”
“I've got the manuals.”
“Of course you have.”

For a while neither of us says anything else. I listen to the room around her. A trolley passes. Someone laughs. A plastic curtain slides along a rail. I would never have chosen a hospital as a place to miss so badly.
“{{firstName}},” she says at last. “I shouldn't have needed you to do this.”
“I know.”
“You can be angry about it.”
“I am.”
She breathes out. I am glad I said it before it became one more thing neither of us could ask.

Wren comes on briefly. She tells me that snow melts at different speeds depending on what I put it on. She has been conducting tests on a windowsill, a glove and the sleeve of Julian's cardigan. He has objected to the cardigan.
Imani is last.
“The chair,” she says.
“Still terrible.”
“Good. Means we're talking to the right person.”
I laugh for the first time since the stairs closed. Miso raises his head to check the sound, then puts it down again.
After the call ends, I find a new line waiting on the board. It is not connected to a person. It has my number written beside it, in handwriting I recognise as my own.
The destination is Friday, 02:13.
I examine the routing stamp. One day after arrival, not the day of departure. The date my phone showed. Nadia's manual calls it a reserved receiving slot.
I've spent two days wondering who was on the other end. Now the empty socket waits for a voice.

I check the return line against Mum's manual before using it. One message, back to the point where the first claim began. The date is a reserved receiving slot, a place in the route rather than a promise about which day the speaker belongs to.
It explains the wrong date on my phone. It does not make hearing my own breathing less strange.
“Whatever happens,” I say, “do not open the door.”
I give myself the notebook. The kitchen drawer. I start one last sentence and the line closes before I know how to finish it.
Miso lifts his head from the blanket.
“Done?”
“I think so.”
“Then somebody's waiting.”
I turn to the next light.

The first week is hard in ways I didn't rehearse. I miss being able to leave a room because I am tired of it. I miss food I can complain about. I miss the sound the flat's radiator makes before it warms up.

Dennis gives me the scores from the match he missed. I bring him a printout and stay while he points out which child is his grandson. The return line cost him a Saturday. It is a small enough debt to remember without turning it into a legend.

Julian and I finish the crossing report before its end date. If I cannot leave the station, he takes my recorded account. The divine office gets the reader or a written account of why we still need it. Anubis sends back a receipt, not a new obligation.
The counter-ledger stays in the archive, available to families challenging the calls they refused. I do not get to decide which of them will use it.

Mum and I close every copy of my private cadence that the station could still reach. Wren listens only as long as she agrees to. I broke one promise about that name; repairing the damage does not make her pretend I kept it.
The return log has all our signatures, including Dennis’s. Nobody can renew the agreement by copying his yes. We file its completed end beside the beginning.

The counter-ledger comes back with scorch marks on its cover. The entries are intact. Julian catalogues the original and the copy separately, so nobody can mistake the correction for the thing it corrected.
I do not miss school until Julian brings my chemistry work through the controlled line. Then I miss the whole building, including the corridor where the lockers never close properly.

Mum calls every evening. Sometimes she talks about the receiving point she is trying to build. Sometimes she tells me what she bought at the supermarket. When she begins explaining an experiment without asking how I am, I interrupt her. The first time, she is hurt. The second time, she catches herself.

Leila keeps the calls from becoming only research. She asks about sleep, then listens when I say I don't know whether I am sleeping or merely resting between messages. She writes it down without pretending the answer is reassuring.

Imani brings a chair. Getting it through the controlled route takes most of a Saturday and an argument with a door which appears not to recognise furniture as an authorised visitor. She refuses to leave it behind. When it finally arrives, the seat is scratched but intact.
“Sit,” she says.
I sit. It is an excellent chair.
She stands beside me for a while, looking at the board. A light comes on, then another. I let them wait. That is permitted now.
“I got the place,” she says.
“At the selection?”
She nods.
I get up so quickly the chair scrapes backwards. She laughs, then I am hugging her, and for a minute the station contains a celebration which has nothing to do with being brave.

Wren visits with Julian. She is learning to write messages which belong only to her. Most are questions. Some are complaints about how many ordinary words have more than one meaning. She brings Miso a knitted mouse. He ignores it until she leaves, then carries it to the blanket.

Voss has not tried to call. The investigation continues above. Nadia has supplied the original manuals and signed a statement about her own work. Julian tells me the records will be complicated. I believe him. I have developed a strong dislike of stories which end when the person responsible looks sad enough.

I help a few callers each day. I turn down requests that would make somebody else answer by force. I ask the right question before accepting a message. Sometimes a receiver refuses. The refusal is recorded, and the line closes. No one is punished for it.
At the end of the third week, Mum reaches the station through the visitor route. Not a voice. A person. She has a bag of sandwiches and several pages of calculations held together by a bulldog clip.
She puts the calculations down first.
“How are you?” she asks.
I look at her hand. It is healing. I look at the sandwiches, the ordinary grease showing through the paper.
“Angry,” I say. “Sometimes. Homesick.”
She sits in the old chair, which Imani repaired rather than throwing away.
“Tell me.”
So I do. Not everything. Enough to begin.

Later, she shows me the calculations. There may be a way to divide the station's role among several consenting operators, each with a defined shift and a way out. It is not ready. It is not a promise she can safely make. She tells me both facts before asking whether I want to help test it.
I read the first page. Make a correction in the margin. Ask a question.
Mum smiles at the familiar impatience in my voice.
On the switchboard, a light comes on. I check its conditions, then lift the receiver.
“Hello,” I say.
Miso closes his eyes in the warm patch beside my new chair. Mum opens her notebook. Somewhere above me, people are having an ordinary evening, and the controlled line home remains open.
THE END
The hallway is empty.
At least, it was when I locked the door.
Then my phone vibrates.
No caller ID.
The call is dated tomorrow.

effects.detail: I answered the first call.
I tried to silence the first call.

beats.text: Before I can follow Miso, Leila catches the torn edge of my coat.
“Turn this out.”
“It's already having a difficult night.”

She doesn't smile. Under Mum's crooked bird patch are three little loops of red thread. I remember her sewing them while I complained about a maths project. One loop is slightly smaller than the others.
“I thought those were bad stitching.”
“They're not good stitching,” Leila says. “They still do the job.”
She puts a piece of string on the table and loops it round the handle of a mug. When she pulls the far end, the mug slides towards the edge. She catches it before it falls.
“A connection can pull you somewhere your body can't follow. These are return protections. If that happens, one can break the claim and bring you back.”
I look at the dressing she has just put on my elbow.
“Does that count?”
“No. A cut is a cut. Don't go jumping off anything to check.”

Three protections. Mum found time to put them in a coat and never found a way to explain why I needed them. I run a finger under the smallest loop. The thread is warm where the rest of the lining is cold.
“Can you make more?”
